title: Possible Russian missile crashes in Poland during Russian attacks on Ukraine
summary: Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least eight people and an apparent Russian missile crashed in Poland, officials said.
story: Kyiv, Ukraine — A Russian ballistic missile and drone barrage across Ukraine overnight into Thursday killed at least eight civilians, including children, and wounded dozens of others, officials said.
The blitz expanded Russia's almost daily bombardment of Ukrainian cities as Moscow apparently looked to exploit Kyiv's critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defenses.
NATO member Poland, meanwhile, was looking into reports that a Russian cruise missile entered its airspace during the onslaught and fell on its territory.

The barrage spanned regions across Ukraine, including western areas near the border with Poland that are far from the front line in the east of the country. Ukraine is believed to store and manufacture weapons for its fight against Russia's more than 4-year-old invasion in the west. Its long-range drones and missiles have battered Russia's oil sector, causing a fuel crisis there.

The attack came two days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Washington with President Trump and representatives of American defense companies, as he pleads for swifter and bigger deliveries of Patriot air defense systems that are the best way to stop Russia's ballistic assaults.

The Iran war has drained stockpiles of the American-made interceptors. President Trump has promised to grant Ukraine licenses to build its own Patriots, but production could take a long time to set up.

"Given the critical shortage of air defense missiles from our partners, our warriors are accomplishing truly incredible things, demonstrating a very high level of professionalism," Zelenskyy said on social media.
"This Russian terror once again proves that protection against the Russian missile threat is the most important task when it comes to saving the lives of our people," he said.
Zelenskyy said at least 10 Ukrainian regions were attacked, with dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities destroyed or damaged.
Russia launched more than 70 missiles, a significant number of them ballistic, he said, along with more than 280 attack drones, of which more than 260 were intercepted.
Polish leader says suspected Russian missile landed in country
A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Poland overnight, violating NATO airspace, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.
Sybiha called it a clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine's air defense is urgent and serves as a guarantee of wider European protection.

The Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces said on X that an unidentified object flying westward in the middle of the night was tracked in Polish airspace and an F-16 fighter jet was launched to identify and intercept it.

The object disappeared from radar screens before it could be identified, the command said. A helicopter flew to its last known location, where the crew discovered a probable impact site in an undeveloped area near the village of Tarnawa-Kolonia in the Lublin province, the command wrote.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk traveled to the area Thursday morning to inspect the site. Later, he said it appeared the object was a Russian missile.

"All the indications are that it was a Russian Kh-101 ballistic missile, but we want to be 100% certain about the type of missile and who launched it," Tusk said during an emergency meeting with other officials. "There was no direct threat because the missile landed in an uninhabited area; we were ready to shoot it down had it continued its flight."

A Ukrainian official, speaking with CBS News reporter Aidan Stretch Thursday on the condition of anonymity, said "it was indeed a KH-101 missile cruise missile that incurred into, into Poland and, and fell there."

"This incident just highlights the need to strengthen Ukraine's air defense very urgently because, of course, if Ukraine had enough air defense capacities, it would shoot down and intercept those missiles before they can even reach allied airspace — NATO airspace —   in neighboring countries."
Details on Russia's strikes in Ukraine
The Russian Defense Ministry said it aimed at Ukrainian air bases, arms factories and military telecommunications and logistics facilities.
The targets included drone production factories and storage depots, a missile plant, an aircraft repair plant, a factory making electronic components, and a chemical plant, it said.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, the Russian attack killed six people and wounded 10, Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said.
Children were among the dead, he said on Telegram - a 6-year-old girl and boys aged 11 and 17.
The children's parents were killed in the same attack, but two more children were pulled alive from under the rubble, Zelenskyy said.
"It was an ordinary home, blown (to) smithereens by a ballistic missile," he said on X.

Russian forces struck the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv with ballistic missiles, killing a 31-year-old man and wounding two others, the National Police press service said. Residential buildings, a market, a garage cooperative, storage facilities and vehicles were damaged in the city, police said.

A cruise missile attack struck the western city of Lviv, wounding 34 people, including three children ages 6, 13 and 15, according to Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv regional military administration. Emergency crews were still searching through rubble.
In the Poltava region, a drone hit company warehouses, killing one person, regional military head Vitalii Diakivnych said.
Ukraine hit back, officials in Russia say
Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight.
A depot belonging to Wildberries online retailer was set ablaze in Russia's Penza region southeast of Moscow, in the latest strike on the company's warehouses, Penza Gov. Oleg Melnichenko.
One person was injured and 200 workers were evacuated, he said.

Wildberries also reported that its warehouse in Sarapul in the region of Udmurtia, more than 600 miles from Ukraine, was struck by a Ukrainian drone and set ablaze. It said the workers had been safely evacuated.
Ukraine accuses Wildberries of supplying goods that can be used by the Russian military.

title: Husband of U.S. woman missing in Grenada doesn't suspect foul play
summary: The husband of a North Carolina woman who went missing last week​ while visiting the Caribbean island of Grenada said Wednesday he believes "there was no foul play" in her disappearance.
story: The husband of a North Carolina woman who went missing last week while visiting the Caribbean island of Grenada said Wednesday he believes "there was no foul play" in her disappearance.

Cailen Waddell, the husband of Elizabeth Waddell, said in a statement that the ongoing investigation will focus on tracing his wife's movements in the hours before she disappeared, adding that "no detail is too small."

Waddell was last seen on security video at around noon on July 22 swimming off Grand Anse Beach, the Royal Grenada Police Force previously reported. According to Cailen Waddell, eyewitnesses later reported interacting with her at about 5:30 p.m. further from shore that same evening.

"After careful and thoughtful consultation with family, local authorities, the U.S. Embassy, and others here in Grenada, I join authorities in believing there was no foul play," Cailen Waddell said in Wednesday's statement. "Liz was last seen swimming in the ocean near Grand Anse, around 5:30 PM, far from shore. She communicated her confidence in her swimming and location, as well as the beauty of the island."

The 44-year-old North Carolina mother was on a three-week vacation with her close friend, Heather, at the time of her disappearance. According to her family, Waddell left the Airbnb she was sharing with Heather, and when she didn't return for hours, Heather went looking for her and found just her towel, but no other sign of her.
A friend of Waddell said this week that surveillance video of her last known movements on the day of her disappearance showed her "floating" and "swimming around."
"But then she, you know, she floats out of the camera view and so that's the last footage of Liz," her friend Amanda Romano-Harmon said.

Surveillance video showed Elizabeth Waddell walking toward a beachside pier around 11:30 a.m. before entering the water and swimming beneath the pier shortly after noon, Royal Grenada Police Acting Police Commissioner Randy Connaught said Tuesday. About 45 minutes later, her friend was seen heading toward the pier before returning alone.
Cailen Waddell described his wife as "a loving free-spirit person," telling Grenadian media last week that his wife "could make friends with anyone and she often did."
Police have asked anyone with information on Waddell's whereabouts to contact authorities immediately. The U.S. State Department has said it is aware of the disappearance.

title: 2 firefighters die in Greece as others fight massive blaze in France
summary: Two firefighters died in a blaze on the Greek island of Crete Wednesday while crews in France confronted a wildfire four times the size of Paris, officials said.
story: Two firefighters died Wednesday while battling a blaze on the Greek island of Crete, officials said, while crews in southern France worked to extinguish a massive, uncontained wildfire that had spread to roughly four times the size of Paris. Across Europe, firefighters confronted a dangerous combination of high temperatures, drought and powerful winds, compromising containment efforts.

The deaths on Crete brought a fatal new dimension to a wildfire emergency stretching from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean. At the peak of the evacuations, a third of a million people were driven from homes and vacation sites in France and Spain.

In France's Gironde region, authorities said the blaze had not spread during a calm night. But temperatures forecast to reach 40 degrees Celsius, or 104 degrees Fahrenheit, and strengthening afternoon winds threatened to turn that respite into only a brief reprieve.

The landscape was so combustible that investigators believe routine brush-clearing work near a high-voltage line may have sparked the inferno, even though the work appeared to comply with regulations.

At the command center in Lège, firefighters bent over maps spread across a car hood, tracking three danger zones: northern Cap-Ferret; the wooded corridor around Marcheprime, Cestas and Saint-Jean-d'Illac; and a military site near Martignas, where a major outbreak forced a large deployment.
More than 2,200 firefighters and over 20 aircraft remained mobilized, backed by crews from across France and European partners.
"We strike quickly and strike hard at any new smoke emissions," Gironde fire commander Matthieu Jomain said.

Beyond the command center, civilians were trying to hold the line themselves. At Souge, volunteers flooded the edges of dirt tracks while a local digger driver plowed through still-burning soil, trying to keep flames from crossing back when the expected west wind arrived. In Lacanau, residents pumped water from a lake into tanks headed for hot spots and firefighters' cisterns.

"If one day the fire starts in our neck of the woods, I know very well that all the people here would do the same for us," said Flavien Dubuch, 33, who drove from Saint-Émilion with his father to help.

Fire crews in France and Spain have battled raging wildfires this summer, which collectively forced more than 300,000 people to evacuate between both countries. In Gironde, more than 250,000 were ordered to evacuate over the weekend, as dry conditions and strong winds began to complicate firefighting efforts. Authorities said the evacuation order was among the largest since World War II.
Hottest day this week
The advance of major fires in the Landes and Var regions has been halted. That left Gironde as France's biggest remaining wildfire battle, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.
Although tens of thousands have been allowed to return home since the evacuation, authorities warned Wednesday that danger could still lie ahead.

Much of the area burned in Gironde is made up of pine forests and scrubland, which grew uncontrollably this year under successive heat waves. The extreme heat that western Europe has experienced in recent months removes moisture from vegetation and lowers humidity, which, in turn, causes grass, brush and forest debris like fallen branches and leaves to burn faster as fuel.
Investigators believe contractors working near a high-voltage line for power-grid operator Enedis ignited the blaze while using a brush-cutting machine, Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul said.

Météo-France said Wednesday would be the hottest and driest day of the week, with elevated wildfire danger across every region of France. Drought now covers mainland France and Corsica, with soils nearing the record dryness reached in August 2022.
Smoke from the Gironde and Landes fires also pushed particulate pollution higher across both departments, regional air-quality monitors said.
Gironde authorities ordered 4,000 more people out of tourist sites along the Atlantic coast on Tuesday, widening what may be France's largest peacetime evacuation.

"The situation remains complicated. That's clear. We're not out of the woods," said Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas, who also authorized 60,000 evacuees to return to three Bordeaux suburbs untouched by fire.
The opposing movements — thousands ordered out of coastal resorts as others returned with mobile phones on and emergency bags packed — captured how precarious the situation remains.
The disruption was spreading beyond the burn zone into Bordeaux's peak tourism season.

Edouard le Grix de la Salle, who runs Château du Grand Verdus with his brother, said official appeals to avoid the region threatened its wine-tourism trade. "How did they not think about protecting that sector?" he told The Associated Press.

At one point the Gironde blaze created a black thundercloud, electrified and lit from within, that generated lightning, violent winds and new fires beyond the original front. The pyrocumulonimbus was the first recorded in France.

Two firefighters died Wednesday while battling a wildfire in the Rethymno region of Crete, Greece's fire department said. They were among about 125 firefighters confronting flames fanned by strong winds, with four helicopters and four water-dropping planes deployed.
The circumstances of their deaths were not immediately clear. The department said they died "in the line of duty to protect the lives and property of citizens and the natural environment."
Tens of thousands begin returning home in Spain
At the height of the crisis, roughly 330,000 people were driven from homes and vacation sites across France and Spain.

Tens of thousands of people began returning home in central Spain after firefighters made progress around Madrid and Ávila. Evacuation orders were lifted for about 20,000 people in the Madrid region, while stay-at-home restrictions ended for another 14,000.
But 10,000 people remain under evacuation orders in Castellón, where a fire was still out of control as Spain braced for its fourth heat wave of the summer.
More than 1,160 square kilometers (448 square miles) have burned across France this year, according to the Interior Ministry.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, warming at more than twice the global average, according to the European Union's Copernicus climate service. Western Europe recorded its hottest June on record, with extreme heat and widespread dryness contributing to the spread and intensification of fires in France and Spain, Copernicus said.

title: Singer-songwriter Glen Hansard killed in motorcycle crash
summary: Academy Award-winning Irish singer-songwriter Glen Hansard has died in a motorcycle crash.
story: Academy Award-winning Irish singer-songwriter Glen Hansard died in a motorcycle crash in Dublin early Wednesday, his management said. He was 56.
"With broken hearts, we announce the passing of Glen Hansard in the early hours of this morning," ATC Management said in a statement to CBS News.

Irish police said a man in his 50s died in a single vehicle motorcycle crash in Lucan on the outskirts of the Irish capital before 4:30 a.m. on Wednesday. The man, who they did not name, was treated at the scene but was pronounced dead a short time later. CBS News partner BBC News reported that police are asking witnesses from the crash to come forward.

Hansard was born in Dublin in 1970, according to the BBC, and busked in the city. He made his acting debut in the 1991 film "The Commitments," playing Outspan Foster, a young working-class member of a Dublin soul band.

Hansard again combined music and acting in the 2007 indie musical film "Once," co-writing the movie's songs with Markéta Irglová. The pair also starred in the film. Hansard and Irglová won the 2008 Oscar for best original song for the number "Falling Slowly." A stage adaptation of the musical ran on Broadway from 2012 to 2015, winning eight Tony Awards, and has played around the world.

Off-screen, Hansard was long-serving frontman for rock band The Frames and performed with Irglová as the rock duo The Swell Season. Hansard has also released five solo albums, including "Didn't He Ramble," which was nominated for a Grammy for best folk album in 2016.

Hansard has made frequent appearances on CBS Saturday Mornings' "Saturday Sessions" segment. In 2015, he showcased "Didn't He Ramble," and in 2018 and 2024 he played songs from other solo albums. In August 2025, he and Irglová performed songs from "Forward," their first album as The Swell Season in 16 years.

At the funeral of The Pogues frontman Shane MacGowan in 2023, Hansard performed The Pogues' song "Fairytale Of New York" with Irish singer Lisa O'Neill, which prompted dancing in the aisles of the church.

For years, Hansard led the Christmas Eve charity busk outside Dublin's Gaiety Theatre, where members of the public gathered to see famous Irish musicians perform in aid of the Dublin Simon Community. The organization said Wednesday it was "devastated" to hear of Hansard's death, according to the BBC.

"While known to many as a genius songwriter and storyteller, for us, he was threefold that, in his generosity, a true advocate for our work and a giant in the fight against homelessness," the Dublin Simon Community said in a statement.
Hansard is survived by his wife and a 3-year-old son. In a 2023 interview with the BBC, Hansard said becoming a father had "completely, in the greatest way possible, upturned everything that I know."
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said he was "deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Glen Hansard."

"A talented musician and actor who made a significant contribution to Ireland's cultural landscape over many years," Martin posted on X, sending his "sincere sympathies to his family, friends and fans."

title: Japan quake toll rises, people still missing in damaged mall and factory
summary: The powerful earthquake that rocked southern Japan has killed at least 18 people and more remain missing in a damaged shopping mall and a paper factory.
story: Kumamoto, Japan — Soldiers and emergency workers combed through a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses looking for trapped survivors Wednesday after a powerful earthquake that killed at least 18 people in southwestern Japan.

The powerful earthquake that hit a day earlier in the Kumamoto area on the southern main island of Kyushu, also left at least 62 people injured, six of them seriously, the prefectural government said. The tally has been steadily growing, fanning fears it may continue to rise. The U.S. Geological Survey measured the quake as a magnitude 6.8.
The sweltering weather heightened worries about the survivors as rescuers braved the heat. It remained unclear how many people might still be missing.
Some of the most serious damage was at the Aeon Mall shopping center in Kashima city, which was bustling with thousands of people when the quake happened.
The company said some 3,000 customers were evacuated to a parking lot before a gas explosion happened in another part of the mall, where some people were still working.
The mall's second floor collapsed, trapping people. Witnesses said the explosion shook the area as much as did the quake.

Aeon Mall president Akio Yoshida told reporters at the site on Wednesday that three people were still missing — all story employees who had been working when the explosion struck. He said three people were confirmed to have been killed in the blast.
"We take it seriously that an explosion happened and precious lives were lost," Yoshida said, bowing deeply along with two other executives.

CBS News correspondent Anna Coren was at the scene on Wednesday as work continued to locate people still trapped inside the structure. She spoke with a man who helped evacuate 200 shoppers, but believed his 23-year-old friend was working inside the mall when the suspected gas explosion went off an hour after the quake.
"I'm worried," he told CBS News. "He's a close friend for a long time, and I'm wanting him to just be safe."

A girl at the scene told Coren that when Kumamoto was last hit by a major earthquake, 10 years ago, she was in an area devastated by the temblor, "but what happened yesterday was so strong, I felt like death was close."
Japanese media aired video of the mall showing part of a ceiling had caved in, and metal parts and other debris were scattered about as helmeted and masked rescue workers searched the area.

In nearby Yatsushino, a chimney collapse at a Nippon Paper Industries factory killed five people while seven others were rescued from the debris, according to the Kumamoto prefectural government disaster team.
Four people were still believed to be trapped there, it said.

Nearly 34,900 homes were still without electricity and some 15,000 homes were without running water, Kumamoto officials said. More than 8,800 people left their homes to stay in more than 400 shelters, where power sources were being added so the evacuation centers had air conditioning.
Aerial police footage showed some homes in residential areas were completely flattened, including a few that crumbled into a nearby river.
Japan's Self Defense Forces are joining rescue workers in the search and rescue operations. Hundreds of professionals were helping with the effort, including firefighters from Taiwan.
"There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it's a race against time," Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said. "We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can."

Takaichi said the federal government was preparing to deliver food and other necessities to hard-hit areas. She also offered her condolences to the victims and sympathy to their relatives, while urging those affected by the quake to take care of themselves under the hot weather.
Bullet train services remained suspended. Although operations at Aso Kumamoto airport resumed Wednesday, some airlines canceled flights as a precautionary measure.
Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that killed at least 50 people. Japan is one of the most quake-prone nations in the world.

title: Kate Middleton is 'indispensable' to royal family as slimmed-down monarchy faces mounting pressure: expert
summary: Royal expert Katie Nicholl calls Kate Middleton "the monarchy's greatest asset," revealing how her cancer journey forged a deeper bond with King Charles.
story: Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says the Princess of Wales won public respect through duty and resilience after health challenges.
Kate Middleton has become one of King Charles' most beloved family members, with one royal expert calling her the "monarchy's greatest asset."

The claim came from Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl, co-host of "The Royals Uncensored." After more than 20 years covering the royal family on tours and engagements, Nicholl said she has spoken to countless palace insiders, many of whom are enchanted by the Princess of Wales.

"I think Catherine, the Princess of Wales, has always been a very valuable asset to the royal family," Nicholl told Fox News Digital. "She is the commoner who married into the royal family ... [She has made] a seamless transition into that unique world of royalty. It's not easy ... There's a huge amount of sacrifice that goes into being a member of the royal family."
PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS

King Charles III kisses Catherine, Princess of Wales, after the Requiem Mass for the Duchess of Kent at Westminster Cathedral in London on Sept. 16, 2025. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the touching moment reflects the increasingly close relationship the monarch shares with his daughter-in-law. (Jordan Pettitt - Pool/Getty Images)
"Catherine's had to give up a huge amount, and yet she does it all with a great deal of grace and dignity, always with a smile," Nicholl said. "So she is absolutely the monarchy's greatest asset."
Nicholl also noted that "the king adores her, and the queen adores her."

Catherine, Princess of Wales speaks with children during an official welcome at the Town Hall on the first day of her visit to Reggio Emilia on May 13, 2026, in Reggio Emilia, Italy. (UK Press via Getty Images)

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that Charles and Kate have forged an even deeper bond since both were diagnosed with cancer. Buckingham Palace announced the king's diagnosis in 2024. In December 2025, Charles shared the "good news" that his treatment would be scaled back in 2026.
WATCH: KATE MIDDLETON IS 'THE MONARCHY'S GREATEST ASSET: EXPERT'

Just weeks after the king's announcement, Kate revealed in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer. She completed chemotherapy that September and announced in January 2025 that she was in remission.
British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that the king, 77, had been greatly inspired by the Princess of Wales' strength.
Catherine, Princess of Wales, Princess Charlotte of Wales and King Charles III during Trooping the Colour on June 15, 2024, in London. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

"King Charles sees enormous value in Princess Catherine," Chard said. "Not just as the wife of his heir, but as the cornerstone of the monarchy itself. He genuinely loves his 'darling' daughter-in-law. His face lights up when he is with her. They share similar interests, and they have shared a similar cancer journey, one that has created a deep bond and understanding that goes beyond duty."

King Charles III and Catherine, Princess of Wales, are seen here at the state banquet for German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and his wife, Elke Budenbender, at Windsor Castle in Windsor, England, on Dec. 3, 2025. (Aaron Chown - Pool/Getty Images)
Chard argued that it hasn't just been Charles who quickly realized that Kate represented the monarchy's future.
"The late queen saw it too," Chard said. "She recognized Catherine's superpowers early on — her ability to listen, find solutions and bring calm to difficult situations."
Queen Elizabeth II, England's longest-reigning monarch, died in 2022 at age 96. (Geoff Pugh)

"King Charles fundamentally views his time on the throne as stewardship," she said. "He sees himself as the caretaker of the institution and is acutely conscious of preparing the next generation. Collaborative preparation between the king and his heir is essential. Having Princess Catherine as the wife of his heir, Charles has struck gold."

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Princess Charlotte, Prince George and Prince Louis watch an RAF flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace after attending Trooping the Colour 2026 on June 13, 2026, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
Royal author Sally Bedell Smith previously told People magazine that Kate is "like the daughter he never had."
"He has always had a very strong bond with her," Smith told the outlet. "He shares with William an impulse to protect her. They are in this together, Kate and the king."

Kate Middleton and the former Prince Charles examine artwork produced on silk during a visit to the Dulwich Picture Gallery on March 15, 2012, in Dulwich, south London, England. (John Stillwell - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
When Kate made her diagnosis public, Buckingham Palace said Charles was "so proud of Catherine for her courage in speaking as he did."

Catherine, Princess of Wales congratulates patient Claire Lorente and her partner, Pablo, as she rings the end-of-treatment bell at the Christie cancer care hospital in Manchester, England, on June 4, 2026. (Andy Stenning - WPA Pool/Getty Images)
Author Christopher Andersen previously wrote in his book "Kate!" that the king was by Kate's side "to lend his cherished daughter-in-law moral support" during her health battle.
Kate's advocacy work following her cancer diagnosis continues, Nicholl told Fox News Digital.
Catherine, Princess of Wales curtseys to King Charles III on Sept. 16, 2025, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Thankfully, despite a serious health issue, she has overcome that," Nicholl said. "We've just seen her climb the three highest peaks in the United Kingdom to raise money for the Royal Marsden. She's turning her experience into something positive, and I think that's earned her a great deal of respect among the British public, along with a lot of love and affection. People are very much behind her and William."

Catherine, Princess of Wales, is seen visiting Evelina London Children's Hospital in London, on July 6, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
Chard echoed those sentiments.

"Princess Catherine connects with people in a way that restores faith in the monarchy," Chard said. "She has learned every aspect of the institution over many years and has blended in carefully without fuss. Princess Catherine is central to the institution's success, and King Charles knows this."

With a slimmed down monarchy, Charles needs key allies now more than ever. His younger brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, stepped back as a working royal in 2019 following his controversial ties to late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Charles has since formally removed Andrew’s princely title and HRH style.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on Feb. 19, 2026, and released after about 11 hours under investigation. He was detained on suspicion of misconduct in public office over allegations that he shared confidential trade reports with Jeffrey Epstein while serving as the U.K.'s trade envoy. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
In 2020, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, stepped back as senior working royals and later settled in California.

From left: Prince William, Kate Middleton, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle attend a ceremony to mark the centenary of the Royal Air Force on the forecourt of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals in 2020. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Princess Anne and other senior working royals are all stretched thin — and none of them are young," author Catherine Mayer previously told People magazine. "William and Catherine carry the whole thing."
Sources told the outlet there had been "even greater attention and expectation on the Waleses." Still, royal experts told Fox News Digital that Kate is well-positioned to support the king.

"Naturally, King Charles recognizes the value of Kate, who is indeed the monarchy's greatest asset," Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "We should add, 'together with her partnership with William and their family.' While we praise Catherine's many strengths, William is the future king. She will one day be queen consort. "William is currently at the center of reports that he and the king differ over how to handle Prince Harry, in particular," Fitzwilliams said. "As she showed when the Sussexes met with the king and Queen Camilla, she fully supports William's approach."

As William and Kate prepare for their future roles, they are likely to remain under close public scrutiny. With Charles' support, royal experts believe the couple is well-positioned for the years ahead.
Prince William is heir to the British throne. (Aaron Chown - Pool/Getty Images)

"It’s not at all surprising King Charles and Princess Catherine have bonded," British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "One can tangibly feel the public also values her wonderful assets from the reception she always receives when in public, as well as in opinion polls. She has become indispensable and has won the public’s trust."

"Charles can depend on Catherine because she is consistent, steady and modern in her approach to family, shaped by her upbringing and dedication to duty," Fordwich said. "She handled the strain of her cancer battle with dignity, without any indication of self-pity."

Catherine, Princess of Wales cools down with a fan as she attends Day 14 of the 2026 Wimbledon Tennis Championships at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club on July 12, 2026, in London. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)
"One can observe from the body language between Charles and Catherine that they are so comfortable together, derived from the time they spent together during their cancer battles."

Mills said working out consistently has saved her from needing hip or knee replacements. (Getty Images)

title: 'Lord of the Rings' star Sean Astin had to sell his home after negotiating 'small' salary for hit movie
summary: Sean Astin reveals he had to sell his house after negotiating a surprisingly small salary for the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy with no residuals.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Sean Astin captured the hearts of fantasy fans everywhere when he starred as Samwise Gamgee in the "Lord of the Rings" but says the compensation was not what one would expect.
In a new interview with The Guardian, the 55-year-old actor shared just how "small" his payday was for the successful Academy Award-winning trilogy.

"I was not prepared for that level of visibility and access," he said. "And there was a disconnect between the attention that I was getting and how much money we had. It was not a lot of money. In fact, I had to sell my house because I negotiated such a small amount on the trilogy."
He revealed in a November 2017 interview on the "Jim and Sam Show" that he made $250,000 for his work on the trilogy in addition to some profit from merchandise sales, but no residuals.
Astin shared that his paycheck for "Lord of the Rings" was not as big as everyone probably thinks. (New Line/courtesy Everett Collection; Frazer Harrison/WireImage)
'MARRIED... WITH CHILDREN' STAR TED MCGINLEY REVEALS HE GETS PENNY RESIDUAL CHECKS FROM HIS HIT TV SHOWS
The "Stranger Things" star said he had purchased a home in Los Angeles and was told he needed to make $250,000 a year to pay the mortgage when he got the role in the films.

"It was an offer for $250,000 for a year and a half," he said. "And I was like, ‘Wait a minute, my pen signed this contract, which obligated me to $250,000 a year, and I’m gonna sign this contract, which will make it so that I absolutely cannot satisfy that other thing.'"
He added that, in the end, it was all about negotiating. He also clarified that by the time the third movie was released, he "was feeling a little bit better" in terms of finances.
"By then, I had done a lot of other work, and we were fine," he added.

Astin's co-star in the first installment of the trilogy, Cate Blanchett, who played Galadriel, also spoke about how little she was paid for her role, telling Andy Cohen in an August 2024 episode of "Watch What Happens Live," "No one got paid anything to do that movie."
Astin said he was paid $250,000 for all three films combined. (JC Olivera/Variety via Getty Images)

Other cast members, including Orlando Bloom and Elijah Wood, have also spoken about how little they were paid for their work in the films, with Bloom telling Howard Stern in 2019 he was paid $175,000 for the trilogy.
Also starring Viggo Mortensen, Sean Bean and Ian McKellen, the trilogy became a huge blockbuster success.
The first film, "Fellowship of the Ring," raked in about $897 million at the worldwide box office, with its sequels bringing in about $945 million and $1.15 billion, respectively.

title: Tim Robbins turns to ayahuasca after feeling 'consumed by anger' over cancel culture
summary: Tim Robbins tells Joe Rogan how an ayahuasca ceremony helped him release years of frustration over cancel culture and political polarization.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Oscar-winning actor Tim Robbins says an ayahuasca trip helped him break free from the anger he felt over America's deep divide.
Robbins revealed the psychedelic experience left him feeling "completely lighter" after years of frustration with cancel culture and political polarization.
The "Shawshank Redemption" star said he turned to the Amazonian psychedelic brew with one goal in mind — to stop being "consumed" by outrage over what he sees as the unraveling of modern society.
KELSEY GRAMMER SUSPECTS HE 'MAY HAVE' LOST HOLLYWOOD ROLES DUE TO CONSERVATIVE VIEWS
Tim Robbins told Joe Rogan how an ayahuasca ceremony helped him release years of frustration over cancel culture and political polarization. (Ernesto Ruscio / Getty Images)

"They tell you to go in with an intention," Robbins said during a candid appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience." "My intention was to … I was frustrated with feeling anger about what was going on in the world, and I said, 'I want to release that. I don't want to be consumed by that anger.'"
Robbins said his psychedelic experience was an intense spiritual journey that included what he described as an encounter with his late mother.
"What she said was, 'You're injured. You're a warrior, and you're injured and you need to rest, but the fight's not over,'" Robbins recalled.
When Joe Rogan asked what battle he believed he was fighting, Robbins pointed squarely at today's culture wars.
Robbins described his intense psychedelic journey that included an encounter with his late mother and left him feeling "completely lighter." (Tristan Fewings / Getty Images)

"I was battling my frustration with the dissolution of society, people being angry at each other over ridiculous things, long friendships being affected, people being canceled for expressing their opinion, all this stuff," he said. "And I wanted out. I wanted to be absolved of that. I didn't want to be engaged in it."
Although Robbins acknowledged skeptics would dismiss the experience, he said it profoundly changed him.
"I definitely felt her presence there. It was no doubt it was her," he said, adding that by the end of the ceremony he felt "completely lighter" and reconnected with his late mother.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
The Oscar-winning actor also compared cancel culture to Soviet Union tactics after Eastern Europe audience members drew parallels to communism. (Presley Ann/Getty Images for TCM)
Earlier in the conversation, Robbins also spoke about the hot-button issue, arguing that cancel culture bears striking similarities to tactics used under the former Soviet Union.
The actor recalled touring Eastern Europe with his play "Topsy Turvy," where he asked audience members in Romania what aspects of modern life reminded them of the communist era.
"They said, 'Without a doubt, cancel culture,'" Robbins recounted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
According to Robbins, audience members described how Soviet authorities allegedly kept damaging personal files on citizens and weaponized them against anyone who stepped out of line.
Morgan Freeman and Tim Robbins starred together in "The Shawshank Redemption." (Paul Archuleta/FilmMagic)

"'Well, Soviet Union used to keep files on all of us, right?'" he recalled the person saying. "'So, as long as you're a good party member, there wouldn't be a thing said. But once you stepped out of line, they brought out that old file. Now that affair with your secretary from 30 years ago is going to ruin your life. They're going to ruin your family. They're going to kill your career. And they're going to make a big public display of it to show other people to stay in line.'"

"They felt like cancel culture was basically operating in the same way as the Soviet Union did," Robbins said. "It was really interesting to see that perspective in Eastern Europe — people that have, you know, lived under that kind of oppressive situation and their perspective on modern day."

Robbins has been a fixture in Hollywood for more than four decades, winning the Academy Award for best supporting actor for 2003's "Mystic River" and starring in films including "The Shawshank Redemption," "Bull Durham" and "Top Gun."
He also founded the Los Angeles theater company The Actors' Gang and has become increasingly outspoken in recent years, criticizing COVID-19 lockdowns and vaccine mandates.

title: Tom Selleck says 'Blue Bloods' cast made major sacrifice to save show before cancellation
summary: Tom Selleck reveals the "Blue Bloods" cast took a 25% salary cut to keep the show going, yet the series still ended despite ranking sixth in ratings.
story: Donnie Wahlberg and Jenny McCarthy told Fox News Digital that they prefer ordering takeout and watching the faith-based TV show for date nights.
Tom Selleck addressed the "very frustrating" end to "Blue Bloods," saying the cast had already taken a 25% salary cut to keep it on the air despite it still ranking in sixth place in broadcast shows.
"They claim 14, but it was 15. We did 15 seasons, 293 episodes," Selleck told Ted Danson on his "Where Everybody Knows Your Name" podcast Wednesday. "’Blue Bloods’ was a labor of love for everybody.

"Maybe people don't realize, but a lot of shows become miserable to work on. You get a lot of egos, and ‘I'm not coming out of my dressing room ‘til he's coming out,’ and it's miserable. It's absolutely miserable."
TED DANSON WAS SHOCKED WOMEN VIEWED HIM AS A SEX SYMBOL DURING EARLY ‘CHEERS’ DAYS
Tom Selleck poses with "Blue Bloods" castmates Bridget Moynahan and Donnie Wahlberg in 2014. (GC Images)
But he said "Blue Bloods" was never like that.
Knowing that his character was the patriarch of the family on the show, he decided to "set an example."

"Either way, everybody got it," he continued, saying that, in the last year of the show, "at our last family dinner, everybody wanted to come back. We'd already taken a 25% cut in salary. We'd already done all sorts of things to keep the show going. But the show was, it was very frustrating 'cause ‘Blue Bloods’ was out of the top 100 shows on broadcast television, ‘Blue Bloods’ was No. 6 in our 15th year."
ROSEANNE BARR HASN’T SPOKEN TO TV SISTER LAURIE METCALF SINCE SHOW’S CANCELLATION
The 81-year-old actor reiterated that "nobody wanted to leave. Everybody was gonna stay on. That's hard to get. It may be some kind of record to have the same cast intact for that length of time."
The cast might have made different decisions if it wasn’t a family, "but, you know, you couldn't very well replace Jamie [Will Estes] or Danny [Donnie Wahlberg] or anybody with another actor."

Tom Selleck filming "Blue Bloods" in 2011. (WireImage)
Two years ago, after shooting the final episode, Selleck told TV Insider he was "frustrated" about the show ending because it was still "wildly successful."

"I’m not going to turn into a bitter old guy saying, ‘Get off my lawn!’ I don’t believe in holding grudges, but if you were to say to the television network, ‘Here’s a show you can program in the worst time slot you got, and it is going to guarantee you winning Friday night for the next 15 years,’ it would be almost impossible to believe," he said at the time.

He added that he felt "Blue Bloods" was "taken for granted because it performed from the get-go. So, how do I feel? It’s going to take a long time to sort all of this out. I remember after the weekend [of the final episode’s shoot], I said, ‘I’ve got to get to bed early tonight because I have to do my dialogue for Monday.’ Well, there was no Monday. It’s just going to take a while."

title: Country star Tracy Lawrence slams California, reveals why he pulled the plug on acting in LA
summary: Tracy Lawrence calls California "disheartening" and reveals $10-a-gallon gas prices make touring the state as unprofitable as going into Canada.

Tracy Lawrence is getting real about why he finds it "disheartening" to visit California.

title: Ella Langley's faith and authenticity fuel record-breaking rise, experts say
summary: Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" surpassed Mariah Carey and Whitney Houston records on the Billboard Hot 100, but her faith-driven rise is just beginning.
story: Country music superstar Ella Langley encouraged fans to not to measure themselves against social media or other people’s expectations during a concert performance.
Ella Langley is making music history without leaving behind the faith, values and traditional sound that first won over fans.

The 27-year-old country star's song "Choosin' Texas" has hit the No. 1 spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart for the 15th nonconsecutive week, surpassing Mariah Carey's 2005 R&B classic "We Belong Together" and Whitney Houston's iconic 1992 power ballad "I Will Always Love You," both of which spent 14 weeks atop the chart, according to a report published by Billboard on Monday.

Langley became the first solo female artist to top the Billboard Hot 100 for that long with a non-holiday song. Mariah Carey's perennial 1994 holiday hit, "All I Want for Christmas Is You," is the only song by a solo female singer to spend more time at No. 1, with 22 weeks atop the chart.
ELLA LANGLEY'S 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SPENDS 15 WEEKS AT NUMBER ONE ON THE BILLBOARD HOT 100
The milestone is the latest achievement in a breakout year that has transformed Langley into one of country music's biggest success stories.
Ella Langley is making music history without abandoning her roots. (SXSW Conference & Festivals via Getty Images)

Beyond the charts, Langley won major industry awards and has expanded her mainstream profile through high-profile brand partnerships, television appearances and recognition from some of country music's most influential artists.
Born in Hope Hull, Alabama, Langley left her hometown in 2019 to move to Nashville, Tennessee, where she spent years writing songs, touring and building a loyal following online.

Langley made her breakthrough with her Riley Green duet "You Look Like You Love Me," which went viral on TikTok, amassed millions of streams on Spotify and Apple Music and introduced her to a wider audience.
The country star's song "Choosin' Texas" has topped the Billboard Hot 100 for 15 nonconsecutive weeks. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
COUNTRY MUSIC STAR RILEY GREEN FIRES UP FANS WITH EPIC NEW SUMMER JAM 'THINK AS YOU DRUNK'

Since then, Langley has emerged as one of country music's most recognizable faces, pairing record-setting commercial success with growing mainstream visibility. The singer recently launched an American Eagle campaign and earned praise from icons, including Shania Twain.
Throughout her rise, Langley has continued to publicly discuss her Christian faith and Alabama upbringing while releasing music firmly rooted in traditional country.
Advertisement
She has frequently thanked God during award speeches, and last month went viral for passionate remarks about faith, Christianity and love during a concert in Lexington, Kentucky.
Langley recently landed a campaign with American Eagle. (Getty Images for American Eagle Outfitters)
While speaking with Rolling Stone last week, Twain described Langley as an "authentic songwriter."
SHANIA TWAIN CALLS ELLA LANGLEY AN 'AUTHENTIC SONGWRITER' WITH A UNIQUE SOUND IN NEW INTERVIEW
"She sounds original," Twain said. "She really does seem very unapologetic."
"That commands respect," Twain added. "I believe what she's saying."

Music and branding experts say those qualities may help explain why Langley has resonated with audiences far beyond country music and why her rise comes at a time when country has become one of America's dominant musical genres.
Shania Twain praised Langley as an "authentic songwriter" and "unapologetic." (Matthew Baker/Getty Images for ABA)
Veteran country music journalist Marcus K. Dowling told Fox News Digital that Langley's appeal isn't a departure from country music's traditions but rather an extension of them.

"Country music has proven that, more often than not, when music, above all else, is rooted in a strong sense of faith, family and fun, it appeals to a lowest and middle common denominator of Americans better than most any other stereotypical American thing," Dowling said.

"Look at the back to back to back moment for Langley," he continued. "It's a tale of how to break a star in on country that's as old as the genre is: A duet with a more established male performer. A discovery, by the genre's fanbase, that her authentically rooted musicality is real, and pairs well with her spotlight-ready cosmetic appeal."

"Then, a song that ties a female performer to an emotive core defined by lovestruck universal yearnings," he added. "From Patsy Cline singing ‘Crazy’ through to Dolly and ‘Jolene,’ Gretchen. Wilson's ‘Redneck Woman’ and more, what Ella's doing has a long lineage of always working when executed with intentionality, honesty, and precision."
Langley made her breakthrough with her Riley Green duet "You Look Like You Love Me." (Theo Wargo/Getty Images)
Doug Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, said Langley's success also reflects what audiences are increasingly looking for in entertainers.

"Humility and self-deprecation go a long way when it comes to connecting with fans," Eldridge said. "In the end, authenticity is a lot like humidity — you can’t see it, but you can feel it; when you do, it’s undeniable."
"Langley has humidity and people embrace that," he added. "At this point, that’s what most of us want: real."
Dowling told Fox News Digital that he believes Langley's rise is emblematic of a broader resurgence that has propelled country music to its greatest level of mainstream popularity in decades.

"We haven't seen country be this pop-dominant in 40 years, dating back to Dolly Parton, Kenny Rogers and the like achieving initial mainstream moments that were almost entirely couched in a very stereotypical brand of blending the Appalachian and Western aesthetics with what, ultimately, country had become as a repository for really great, crossover-friendly pop music," he said.
Langley has continued to frequently speak out about her faith. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)
Eldridge argued that country's recent dominance is not surprising because its songs often center on universal experiences.

"Most of the artists are singing about topics that the majority of Americans can relate to: loving your family, being proud of your country, first love, lost love, struggling with bills, trying to be a better person, and giving thanks to Jesus," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"This has been the foundational basis for American vision, values and virtues for a long time," Eldridge added. "Others are just waking up to that reality."
Langley's growing mainstream appeal has drawn comparisons to Taylor Swift's crossover from her country music beginnings to global pop stardom.
However, Eldridge pointed to what he views as a key difference between the two artists.
The singer's rise has drawn comparisons to Taylor Swift's early career crossover. (Andre Dias Nobre/AFP via Getty Images)
"Langley is more true to country music, than Swift ever was in her early days," Eldridge said. "That said, Swift built an audience — and later, an empire — so she knew what she was doing all along."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Eldridge told Fox News Digital that it is too early to know whether Langley will ultimately follow Swift's trajectory or reach the same level of commercial success. He also pointed out that Swift is far from the first country-pop crossover star.

"Swift deserves all the credit for her self-built, billion-dollar empire, but assigning her sole attribution for the country-pop cross-over is looking past all those artists who successfully built that model and passed down the blueprint," he said.
PR expert Doug Eldridge said Langley should stick to her roots rather than pursue a full pop crossover. (Ethan Miller/Reuters)
Eldridge argued Langley may be better served by continuing to lean into the country sound and faith-based identity that have defined her career rather than pursuing a full-fledged pop crossover.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Langley has both commercial appeal and a sense of authenticity — it’s hard to maintain both once you fully commit to the pop cross-over," he said.
"Historically speaking, country artists have careers; pop artists have a moment."
Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

title: Zac Brown Band's John Driskell Hopkins says he's 'chasing the clock' after ALS diagnosis
summary: John Driskell Hopkins says he's "chasing the clock" since his 2021 ALS diagnosis, still touring with Zac Brown Band while planning for 2027.
story: John Driskell Hopkins told Fox News Digital that he's been trying to fit in as much as possible since his diagnosis in 2021.
Zac Brown Band's John Driskell Hopkins is opting to look at his ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) diagnosis in a different light and is trying to make everyday count.

Over a decade after the Ice Bucket Challenge surfaced on social media, it is making a comeback. During an interview with Fox News Digital about the challenge, Hopkins explained that after his diagnosis in 2021, he's been "chasing the clock" ever since.

"I'm almost busier now than I was before because I'm trying to get so much done. I'm tryin' to fit it all in. I'm taking more family vacations. I'm in the studio more than I should be. I'm still on tour with Zac Brown Band right now. You know, my fingers work. My voice works, it's been compromised, but most of the set, no one would notice," Hopkins, a founding member of Zac Brown Band, said.
John Driskell Hopkins of Zac Brown Band was diagnosed with ALS in 2021. (Derek White/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)

He continued, "And I'm playing different things on stage, but they still don't make sense. You know, I'm chasing the clock more than I ever have been. And what I worry about is that that is causing me stress, which might be exacerbating my condition. So it's a bit of a catch-22, you know, I've created."
ZAC BROWN BAND'S JOHN DRISKELL HOPKINS FIGHTS ALS DIAGNOSIS: ‘CRYING SUCKS’
Acknowledging the reality of his diagnosis, Hopkins said that he's looking toward the future where he might not be able to sing.
"I hope that my progression continues to be slow and that I can sing for a long time, but who knows?" he said.

In 2014, Hopkins and the Zac Brown Band participated in the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge on social media – years before his diagnosis. At the time, Hopkins had no idea what the disease was, let alone that he would be diagnosed one day.
"I'm chasing the clock more than I ever have been."
WATCH: Zac Brown Band's John Driskell Hopkins is 'chasing the clock' after ALS diagnosis

"I didn't even know what it was. I mean, I think a lot of people in the band that did the challenge with me understood that it was neurological and fatal, but we didn't have any clue as to how it affected the body more," he began.

"Certainly not how cases were increasing. I mean, we have seen an explosion of neurodegenerative diseases and I can only, generally point to maybe its toxicity. You know, maybe in the world where we're just consuming a lot more things that are doing us harm. That's all I can guess. But I would have never thought… I was indestructible in 2014, you know?"

With several notable public figures recently diagnosed with ALS, the Ice Bucket Challenge has begun resurfacing across social media. Hop and his team at Hop On A Cure have now joined in, sharing their own Ice Bucket Challenge video and passing the challenge on to fellow ALS organizations, as well as the Zac Brown Band.
MICHAEL J. FOX SAYS GOING PUBLIC WITH PARKINSON'S WAS 'HELL' ON WIFE TRACY POLLAN

Hopkins told Fox News Digital he's glad the trend has come back around this summer. Hopkin's nonprofit organization and the Zac Brown Band posted videos on Instagram in July participating in the challenge.
"It's very popular, and it's fun in the summer. It's been a really hot summer this year, all over the world. And we were in London with 95 degree days, and they never see that," Hopkins said.
John Driskell Hopkins and wife Jennifer started the nonprofit, Hop On a Cure, in 2022. (Emilee Chinn/Cincinnati Reds)
When asked how he's been able to stay strong during his diagnosis, Hopkins told Fox News Digital that he doesn't feel strong at all.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I don't feel strong, people often ask me where my strength comes from, but I feel incredibly weak, not just physically. You know, I'm an actor, I have a theater degree, so I'm acting strong," he said.
WATCH: John Driskell Hopkins talks about the viral ALS Ice Bucket Challenge

Hopkins was diagnosed with ALS just before Christmas in 2021 and announced his diagnosis in May 2022. After his diagnosis, Hopkins and his wife, Jennifer, founded the nonprofit organization, Hop On A Cure, to help accelerate research to prevent, reverse and ultimately cure ALS while also raising awareness and supporting families affected by the disease.
At the time of his diagnosis, Hopkins emphasized that his disease had been slowly progressing, allowing him to continue touring and performing with the band.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
During his interview with Fox News Digital, Hopkins said he's in a different position than 99% of ALS patients because he is still able to plan for the next calendar year.
John Driskell Hopkins feels fortunate to still be planning for 2027 amid his ALS diagnosis. (ANGELA WEISS/AFP via Getty Images)

"The fact that I still see next year in my future puts me in a different position than 99.9% of ALS patients. The fact that I'm looking to my calendar for '27. I'm gonna be at the 30a Songwriters Festival '27, and maybe I won't be able to sing what I can now, but maybe I will, you know, we just don't know, and I appreciate you recognizing that reaction as strength, but to me, it's getting up every day that I can and doing what I do," Hopkins concluded.

title: George and Amal Clooney evacuate France home as wildfires spread across Europe
summary: George and Amal Clooney sent a letter to the Brignoles mayor before evacuating, saying they have "no idea" if their home will survive the fires.
story: Wildfires are sweeping across Spain and France, forcing more than 250,000 people to evacuate. One blaze is threatening France's famed Bordeaux wine region, while Spain has declared a national emergency. France has deployed the military, and the Tour de France has been shortened as firefighters battle the massive blazes.
A representative for George Clooney confirmed the evacuation to People and shared a letter the couple sent to Brignoles Mayor Didier Brémond

The couple and their 9-year-old twins left their home in Brignoles, in France's Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region, as fires threatened large swaths of the Mediterranean, the outlet reported. A representative for George Clooney confirmed to People that the couple sent a letter to Brignoles Mayor Didier Brémond before leaving.
"Dear Didier, At this point we have no idea whether our beautiful home makes it through this terrible moment," the letter began.
DEADLY FRENCH WILDFIRES THREATEN MISSILE PLANTS, NUCLEAR SITES AS FOURTH HEATWAVE LOOMS
George and Amal Clooney reportedly evacuated their home in southern France as fast-moving wildfires spread across parts of Europe. (Joe Maher; AP Photo/Emma Da Silva)

"As we evacuate Brignoles we want to emphasise 2 things, first we hope you and the people of our city are safe and second that Amal and i are committed to making sure that whatever happens to our village, we are part of this community and we’ll be part of making it whole," the letter continued. "We love Brignoles and our friends who live there."
Fox News Digital has reached out to Clooney's representatives for additional comment, including whether the family has safely evacuated and if there is any update on the condition of their home.
The evacuation comes as wildfires continue to scorch southern Europe.
EUROPE'S FIRES REVEAL DEADLY MIX OF RECORD HEAT, HUMAN ERROR, ARSON AND LAND MISMANAGEMENT
George and Amal Clooney reportedly left their home in Brignoles, France, as wildfires spread across the region, according to People. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images for History)

As of Wednesday, an uncontained wildfire roughly four times the size of Paris was burning across southwestern France.  The blaze was separate from the fire threatening the Brignoles area, where about 3,000 people were evacuated. Fires also continued to threaten parts of southern Europe, and three firefighters died in Greece as crews battled extreme heat, drought and strong winds, according to The Associated Press.
More than 300,000 people have been forced to evacuate in France and Spain, including residents and tourists.

Temperatures climbed to nearly 104 degrees Wednesday in France's Gironde region, where the country's largest wildfire prompted the evacuation of roughly 220,000 residents and vacationers at its peak. While many have since returned, tens of thousands remain displaced.
HEATHER LOCKLEAR SAYS SHE LIVES 'FAR AWAY' FROM HOLLYWOOD AND STAYS OUT OF THE SOCIAL SCENE
Clooney and his family spend much of their time on a farm in France. (Christopher Anderson/Esquire)
In an October 2025 interview with Esquire , Clooney said he and Amal chose to raise their family on a farm in France to give their children a quieter upbringing away from Hollywood.

"A good portion of my life growing up was on a farm, and as a kid, I hated the whole idea of it," he said. "But now, for them, it’s like—they’re not on their iPads, you know? They have dinner with grown-ups and have to take their dishes in. They have a much better life."

Clooney also said he was "worried about raising our kids in L.A., in the culture of Hollywood."

"I felt like they were never going to get a fair shake at life," he said. "France — they kind of don’t give a s--- about fame. I don’t want them to be walking around worried about paparazzi. I don’t want them being compared to somebody else’s famous kids."

title: Megan Moroney cancels show mid-performance, leaves stage in tears
summary: Megan Moroney called canceling her Denver concert at Ball Arena "the hardest decision" she's ever made. The show is rescheduled for Aug. 27.
story: Country music star Megan Moroney told Fox News Digital she is not ‘emotionally available’ for a romantic relationship, putting all her energy into her music career.
Country star Megan Moroney cut her Denver concert short Tuesday night after becoming too sick to continue performing, later telling fans it was "the hardest decision" she has ever had to make.
The singer took the stage at Ball Arena but struggled through just three songs before stopping the show. Moroney returned to address the audience herself, apologizing as she fought back tears.
"I am obviously extremely sick, and I thought I did everything to make myself better, and obviously, two songs in, I just can't play this show tonight," she told the crowd in a fan-recorded video.
JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK
Fan-recorded video captures Megan Moroney fighting back tears as she stops her Denver Ball Arena show after just three songs due to illness. (Photo by Rick Kern/Getty Images for CMT)
MEGAN MORONEY STUNS IN ORANGE BIKINI DURING FRIEND'S BAHAMAS BACHELORETTE
Despite ending the performance early, Moroney assured concertgoers she planned to make up for the disappointing night.
"I want to give you guys the show you deserve. ... I'm sorry," she said.
Fans inside the arena responded with encouragement, with one audience member shouting, "That's OK Meg, I love you," as the visibly emotional singer exited the stage.
Ball Arena later confirmed the concert had been canceled because Moroney was feeling under the weather.
The "Am I Okay?" singer shared an emotional Instagram message after ending her concert early, promising Denver fans a rescheduled date. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images)
"Megan is unable to continue her performance this evening due to illness, and we must end the show at this time," the venue said in a statement.
"Please allow event staff to direct you to the nearest exit, and we will follow up with more information as soon as we're able."
COUNTRY SINGER MEGAN MORONEY SWEARS OFF DATING AFTER MEN 'RUINED' HER BIGGEST MOMENTS
Moroney apologized to fans for canceling her Denver show, saying she was unable to perform at 100% and announcing the concert has been rescheduled. (Megan Moroney/Instagram)
The venue added that updates would be posted on its website and apologized "for the inconvenience" while thanking fans for their understanding and cooperation.
Shortly after, Moroney shared an emotional message with fans on Instagram, explaining that continuing the concert would have meant delivering a performance below her own standards.
"That was the hardest decision I've ever had to make & I'm so sorry to cancel the show tonight," she wrote.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"I never ever will give you guys a show that is not 100% and by song 3 I knew that I was not capable of giving that to you tonight."
The "Am I Okay?" singer said she was devastated by the decision, adding, "I'm typing this as I'm quite literally bawling my eyes out in my dressing room & it hurts me so much to disappoint you all."

Moroney also announced that the Denver concert has been rescheduled for Aug. 27. Tickets purchased for Tuesday night's performance will be honored for the new date, and fans unable to attend can request refunds through their original point of purchase.
"I've never had to do this & I'm truly so sorry," she wrote before closing her message with, "i love u guys."
Fox News Digital reached out to Moroney for comment.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
After leaving college, she moved to Nashville. Moroney's "Tennessee Orange" breakthrough helped transform her into an award-winning country sensation. (John Shearer/Getty Images for CMT)
The abrupt cancellation comes as Moroney continues touring following the success of her third album and a string of sold-out performances across the country.
Her emotional apology and promise to return were met with widespread support from fans online, many of whom encouraged the singer to focus on recovering before getting back on stage.
Despite the canceled show, Moroney's music career continues to soar.
After attending the University of Georgia, she moved to Nashville to pursue music full time.

Her 2022 breakout hit, "Tennessee Orange," launched her into the country music spotlight, and she has released three albums since: "Lucky" (2023), "Am I Okay?" (2024) and "Cloud 9" (2026).
Moroney also earned ACM and CMA honors as the country's top new female artist before releasing her latest project, "Cloud 9," in February and launching her current tour in May.

GISELE BÜNDCHEN CELEBRATES BIRTHDAY IN LEOPARD-PRINT BIKINI AS SHE REFLECTS ON GRATITUDE

title: Willie Nelson urges Americans to fight 'water thieving' AI data centers devouring rural Texas farmland
summary: Willie Nelson urges Americans to fight data centers invading rural Texas land, warning of light pollution and water thieving near his Abbott home.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Willie Nelson urged Americans to think again when it comes to building the future.
Nelson, 93, encouraged followers to "fight against data centers invading our land" in a social media plea shared Tuesday.
The country music legend reflected on being able to see "stars at night" in his Texas hometown, but that light pollution and "water thieving" were imminent in a looming industrial climate.
KACEY MUSGRAVES ABRUPTLY CANCELS CONCERT DATES FROM 'MIDDLE OF NOWHERE' TOUR
Willie Nelson pleaded with his followers Tuesday to focus on the environmental impacts of data farming centers. (Peter Pakvis)
"I grew up in Abbott, and I still have a home there with farmed land where I can still see stars at night," Nelson told his followers.
"And now our community, like many others, needs to fight against data centers invading our land.
SINGER ZACH TOP SLAMS MODERN COUNTRY MUSIC, SAYS IT LACKS 'SOUL'
"The last thing we need is a loud, water thieving, light polluting, data center anywhere near our town (or any others for that matter)."
The "On the Road Again" singer noted how "the strength of rural America has never come from big industrial footprints."
A post shared by Willie Nelson (@willienelsonofficial)

"It comes from generations of people, open spaces, local businesses, and a connection to the land," Nelson wrote. "All of America deserves thoughtful stewardship that doesn’t steal farmland (where our essential shared-food is grown) and small family farmers’ livelihoods, and not data centers that only destroy the environment around them.

"Whoever controls food and water, controls the masses. Let’s not allow our own demise or give up control over necessary resources in the U.S. and especially in Abbott."
The legendary country singer reflected on the need for "thoughtful stewardship that doesn't steal farmland." (Rick Kern)
Nelson's a longtime environmental advocate and has raised more than $90 million through his Farm Aid nonprofit, which he co-founded with John Mellencamp and Neil Young more than four decades ago.
The charity was first formed in 1985 to raise awareness about the loss of family farms and to raise funds to keep farm families on the land.
On Tuesday, Gov. Greg Abbott called for a ban on data center developments in rural Texas.

title: Jared Leto responds to sexual misconduct allegations made by multiple women in explosive documentary
summary: Jared Leto denies sexual assault allegations from four women who claim offenses occurred when they were teenagers, calling the claims "categorically false."
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Jared Leto is denying allegations of criminal sexual conduct after four women accused the Oscar-winning actor and musician of offenses they claim occurred when they were teenagers.
"I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life," Leto said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital. "These claims are absolutely and categorically false."

The allegations are detailed in the new BBC documentary, "Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret," which premiered Wednesday. The film features interviews with 10 participants, nine of whom shared their stories publicly for the first time.
According to the documentary, four women allege Leto engaged in criminal sexual conduct between 2002 and 2016, when the actor and Thirty Seconds to Mars frontman — now 54 — was in his 30s and 40s.
JASON ALEXANDER APOLOGIZES AFTER COURTNEY STODDEN SAYS 2012 COMEDY SKETCH OBJECTIFIED HER AS A MINOR
Jared Leto has denied allegations of sexual misconduct, telling Fox News Digital the claims are "categorically false." (Christopher Polk/Variety via Getty Images)

In a BBC story published Wednesday, one woman alleged she had sex with Leto at his California home when she was 17 years old. According to the outlet, the woman said Leto, who was 34 at the time, dismissed concerns after they discussed California's age of consent being 18.
"It wasn't a huge concern for him," she alleged. "He told me, 'I would like you to call me daddy.' And it was either pretend to be a little girl or 'my little girl.'"
The woman said that because she was "so naive and vulnerable" at the time, she didn't understand that this behavior wasn't "normal" in an adult relationship.
"It was only as time went on that I realized more and more how scary that really was," she said.
OSCAR WINNER JARED LETO ADMITS DEPTHS OF DRUG ADDICTION: 'IT TOOK ME FOR A RIDE'
A second woman alleged Leto sexually assaulted her in what she described as a "dingy gross motel" in Las Vegas in 2002, saying he invited her there after meeting her at the store where she worked.
According to the documentary, the woman said Leto called her into the bathroom while he was showering.
Multiple women have alleged sexual misconduct against Leto, four of whom were teens at the time.  (Mike Marsland/WireImage)
"I don't think there was many words exchanged, and he opened the shower curtain and started kissing me," she alleged.
She claimed Leto then grabbed her hand and forced her to masturbate him.
"Most of my life I had viewed this event as, I was a stupid girl … and so this bad thing happened," she said.
A third woman alleged Leto threatened her with sexual assault after inviting her to a hotel room in London after a Thirty Seconds to Mars concert in 2013.

The former model said she was 19 at the time but told Leto she was 17 because she "felt the need" to pretend to be younger to protect herself. After telling Leto she was 17, the woman claimed he said, "Age is just a number, and, anyway, we're in Europe."
JARED LETO RECALLS ‘NEARLY DYING’ WHILE ROCK CLIMBING
The woman claimed one of Leto's assistants encouraged her to join in on another party at a nearby hotel room. However, when she arrived, she realized there was no party.
Ten participants spoke about their experiences with Leto in a new BBC documentary.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images for MTV)
"I get into the hotel room, it's really dark and then I see that it's just him," she said. "Weren't there supposed to be other people?"
The woman claimed she asked Leto for a phone charger or some cash to get home, but he dismissed her requests.

After asking if she could sleep on a chaise lounge because she had no way home, the woman claimed Leto repeatedly told her she would wake up "with a d--- in her ass."
After realizing she "was not safe," the woman left the room.
A fourth woman said Leto began grooming her when she was 16, made repeated sexually explicit phone calls to her and on at least one occasion suggested the two have sex.

According to the BBC, the woman was later presented with a nondisclosure agreement intended to prevent her from discussing her alleged relationship with Leto. She declined to sign the document, which BBC said it had reviewed.
Leto reportedly did not respond to requests for comment during the making of the documentary. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
Additional women also accused the actor of making what they described as "strange" and sexually explicit phone calls while they were underage or teenagers.

The documentary also featured interviews with two former employees connected to Thirty Seconds to Mars, who claim staff members were uncomfortable with Leto's interactions with teenage girls.
One former employee alleged Leto would invite teenage girls backstage to his dressing room or to a house where the band was recording.
"I think everyone thought the age gap was way too big," the former employee said.
The allegations are the latest in a series of claims against the Academy Award winner.

In June 2025, Air Mail published interviews with nine women who alleged Leto engaged in inappropriate sexual behavior over the years, including accusations involving minors. Those allegations included claims that Leto asked sexually explicit questions to a 16-year-old, exposed himself to a 17-year-old and placed an 18-year-old's hand "on him."
The Thirty Seconds to Mars frontman was in his 30s and 40s at the time of the alleged allegations.  (Lia Toby/Getty Images)
The Air Mail report followed allegations by Los Angeles DJ Allie Teilz, who publicly claimed she was assaulted by Leto when she was 17.
At the time, representatives for Leto "expressly" denied the Air Mail allegations, calling Teilz's claims "demonstrably false."
