title: Millions could gain easier access to popular peptides after FDA panel vote
summary: An FDA panel voted to recommend six peptides including BPC-157, TB-500, and KPV for compounding by licensed pharmacies instead of grey market vendors.
story: Dr. Alex Tatem, a board-certified urologist in Indiana, discusses why upcoming federal hearings on seven peptides were mandated and argues that years of patient use show a promising safety profile.
An FDA advisory committee has voted by a majority to recommend broader access to certain peptides.
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that help regulate functions such as metabolism, growth and tissue repair, according to Cleveland Clinic.

Some peptides are used in FDA-approved medications, including insulin and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, while others are experimental compounds marketed for wellness or performance that remain under federal review.
FDA TO REVIEW 7 POPULAR PEPTIDES TOUTED FOR WEIGHT LOSS, HEALING AND LONGEVITY

Seven peptides were reviewed during a two-day hearing held by the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee in Maryland last week. The panel considered whether each peptide should be added to the Section 503A Bulks List.
If ultimately approved by the FDA, licensed compounding pharmacies could prepare them for valid prescriptions instead of leaving patients to rely on unregulated online vendors.
Peptides have surged in popularity for weight loss, muscle building, performance enhancement, chronic disease management and even wound repair. (iStock)
The committee voted in favor of loosening restrictions on the following six peptides, according to Reuters.

BPC-157: Proposed to treat ulcerative colitisTB-500: Proposed for wound healingKPV: Proposed for wound healing and inflammatory conditionsMOTS-c: Proposed to treat obesity and osteoporosisSemax: Proposed to treat cerebral ischemia (a shortage of blood flow and oxygen to the brain), migraine and trigeminal neuralgia (a chronic pain condition in the face)Epitalon: Proposed to treat insomnia
BPC-157: Proposed to treat ulcerative colitis
TB-500: Proposed for wound healing
KPV: Proposed for wound healing and inflammatory conditions
MOTS-c: Proposed to treat obesity and osteoporosis
Semax: Proposed to treat cerebral ischemia (a shortage of blood flow and oxygen to the brain), migraine and trigeminal neuralgia (a chronic pain condition in the face)
Epitalon: Proposed to treat insomnia
The Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted in favor of moving six peptides forward. (iStock)

While some peptide experts celebrate this as one step closer to access to life-improving drugs, others claim there isn’t enough data on safety and efficacy. The FDA will now consider the committee's recommendation before making a final decision.
Jim LaValle, a Texas-based clinical pharmacist and chair of the International Peptide Society, who testified at the hearings, noted that restrictions still exist.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This was not FDA approval, nor was it a blanket endorsement of every peptide, every use or unrestricted access," LaValle, who is also a board-certified nutritionist, told Fox News Digital. "I have said throughout this process that you do not solve a quality problem by forcing the market underground."

"I was encouraged by the committee’s recommendation because it creates an opportunity to move patients away from unverified research use only (RUO), otherwise known as grey market products, and toward a more accountable medical pathway."
The "right model" is access with guardrails, qualified clinicians, licensed pharmacies, validated quality testing and "meaningful" patient follow-up, an expert told Fox News Digital. (iStock)
LaValle said his work with the International Peptide Society focuses on training clinicians about the potential benefits and risks of peptide therapies as interest in the compounds grows.
The "right model" is access with guardrails, qualified clinicians, licensed pharmacies, validated quality testing and "meaningful" patient follow-up, according to the expert.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"My hope is that the FDA follows the recommendation with a transparent, science-driven process; establishes clear, peptide-specific standards; and follows the guidance for approving a substance that meets the FDA’s current regulations," LaValle said.
This process includes checking that both the active ingredient and the final product meet quality standards, and setting up a system for tracking and reporting any side effects.

"The peptide revolution is here," LaValle said. "However, don’t expect miracles. Better choices related to diet, exercise, gut health, sleep, stress and managing metabolic health, guided by regular lab assessments, should be the goal."

"My hope is that the FDA follows the recommendation with a transparent, science-driven process; establishes clear, peptide-specific standards; and follows the guidance for approving a substance that meets the FDA’s current regulations," an expert said. (Photo by ISSAM AHMED/AFP via Getty Images)
"In some cases, peptides can play an important part on the journey of performance aging and repair," he went on. "The American public should understand that nothing changed overnight."
LaValle emphasized that the advisory committee's vote was only a recommendation, not a final FDA decision, and noted that compounded medications are regulated differently than FDA-approved drugs.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"The evidence is also not equally mature across all peptides that are approved by the FDA," he noted. "People should avoid products sold online as ‘research use only’ and should not self-experiment."
"Any consideration of peptide therapy should involve a qualified licensed clinician and a legitimate licensed pharmacy."
Putting peptides into practice

Board-certified internist and longevity expert Dr. Amanda Kahn expressed her particular interest in MOTS-c because of its "potential role in mitochondrial biology and metabolic health," as mitochondrial dysfunction is associated with aging and many chronic diseases.

"It’s an exciting area of research and I think therapies targeting cellular metabolism deserve continued scientific attention," the New York-based expert told Fox News Digital. "What excites me isn’t a regulatory decision itself. It’s the opportunity to better understand therapies that may help patients."
The clinician said she incorporates select peptides into her own practice "when appropriate with informed consent and careful monitoring."

"I’m always looking for more data that helps us better identify which patients are most likely to benefit," she said. "I encourage patients to approach all investigational peptides with the same level of caution – many have compelling mechanistic or pre-clinical data, but human evidence remains limited."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Although many of these peptides are "supported by a compelling biological rationale," Kahn stressed that treatment decisions should be individualized and "made with a physician who understands both the potential benefits, risks and uncertainties."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Is drinking every day alcoholism? Experts explain where culture and addiction collide
summary: Ed Sheeran's viral podcast clip reignites debate over British drinking culture versus American alcoholism definitions and when drinking becomes a problem.
story: Fox News medical contributor Dr. Nicole Saphier joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to weigh in on new dietary guidance surrounding alcohol consumption as the overall drinking rate hits a new low.

A clip from Ed Sheeran's appearance on "The Louis Theroux Podcast" has recently resurfaced on social media, sparking renewed debate over differences between British and American attitudes toward alcohol.
"Americans call something ‘alcoholism’ that Brits simply call ‘culture.’ Maybe one or two pints at the end of a workday," the singer said during the 2025 podcast.
"On a Friday you’ll have 6 pints and a bottle of wine. It’s not alcoholism to drink every day here … It’s just the culture."
NIGHTLY GLASS OF WINE MAY NOT BE AS HARMLESS AS MANY PEOPLE THINK, STUDY SUGGESTS
Americans and Britons consume similar amounts of alcohol overall, with the average adult drinking about 9.7 liters of pure alcohol per year, according to the World Health Organization.

Drinking patterns — such as how often people drink, how much they consume in a single sitting and social attitudes toward alcohol — can differ even when overall consumption is similar, according to public health experts.
Americans and Britons consume similar amounts of alcohol overall, with the average adult drinking about 9.7 liters of pure alcohol per year, according to the World Health Organization. (iStock)

In the U.K., pubs are commonly regarded as community gathering places, with alcohol representing a routine part of social life for many people. In the U.S., attitudes toward drinking tend to vary more widely by region, religion and social norms, experts say.
Jessica Steinman, chief clinical officer at No Matter What Recovery in Los Angeles, noted that British and American cultures have always been very different, and that includes alcohol consumption.
DRINKING ALCOHOL MAY INFLUENCE CRAVINGS FOR CERTAIN FOODS IN A SURPRISING WAY, STUDY SUGGESTS

"Americans can’t legally drink until 21, and it is frowned upon to do so before that age," she told Fox News Digital. "In England, there is less stigma and restrictions around alcohol, which changes how people view it and drink it."
When does drinking become alcohol use disorder?

"Regardless of where anyone lives and regardless of their culture, when alcohol or substances start negatively affecting someone’s life or when someone cannot control the levels of alcohol they drink, then it is a problem," Steinman said.

"When drinking gets in the way of a job, school or relationships — or when people start numbing out from difficult feelings or escaping their problems through alcohol — it isn’t just cultural drinking, it’s an addiction."
In the U.S., attitudes toward drinking tend to vary more widely by region, religion and social norms, experts say. (iStock)

Steinman said she's concerned that people with alcohol use disorder may dismiss or justify their drinking as a normal part of their local culture, making them less likely to recognize it as a problem and seek help.

Chris Tuell, EdD., clinical director of addiction services at Lindner Center of HOPE and associate professor at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, reiterated that Sheeran’s comments highlight how culture influences people’s perceptions of alcohol.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"What is considered ‘normal’ in one country may seem excessive in another," he told Fox News Digital. "In parts of the U.K., Ireland, Germany, Australia or even parts of the U.S., drinking is woven into sporting events, celebrations, work gatherings and family traditions."
Tuell noted, however, that culture does not determine whether someone has alcohol use disorder (AUD).
"When drinking gets in the way of a job, school or relationships ... it isn’t just cultural drinking, it’s an addiction."

"The fact that something is common does not automatically make it healthy — the same principle applies to alcohol," he told Fox News Digital. "A person may live in a culture where drinking every evening is expected. Another person may rarely drink because their culture discourages alcohol altogether. Neither person's cultural background alone tells us whether alcohol is helping or hurting them."
Two people can drink exactly the same amount each week while having completely different outcomes, according to Tuell.
Whether someone drinks every day, only on weekends or only at celebrations is only part of the picture, an expert noted. (iStock)

"One person may drink socially, maintain healthy relationships, perform well at work and easily choose not to drink when needed," he said. "Another person drinking the exact same amount may experience worsening anxiety, strained relationships, poor sleep, financial problems, declining health and an inability to stop."
Whether someone drinks every day, only on weekends or only at celebrations is only part of the picture, the expert noted.

Warning signs to watch for
Tuell recommends paying close attention to the following important patterns that can potentially indicate alcohol use disorder.

Having difficulty controlling drinkingDrinking more than intendedSpending increasing amounts of time obtaining or recovering from alcoholContinuing to drink despite relationship problemsContinuing to drink despite medical problemsContinuing to drink despite worsening depression or anxietyGiving up important activities because of drinkingDrinking in dangerous situationsDeveloping a higher tolerance to alcoholExperiencing withdrawal symptoms
Having difficulty controlling drinking

"Ultimately, AUD is measured less by how much a person drinks and more by how much alcohol has begun to take from their life," Tuell said.

"That perspective moves us beyond stereotypes and cultural expectations. It replaces judgment with curiosity, stigma with understanding, and shame with the opportunity for honest self-reflection and meaningful change."
Anyone experiencing symptoms of alcohol use disorder should consult a healthcare provider for evaluation and guidance. (iStock)

One of the greatest barriers to recognizing a drinking problem is comparison, according to the expert — as people might say things like "everyone I know drinks this much" or "my family drinks every day."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Those comparisons can be misleading," Tuell said. "Imagine someone saying, ‘everyone in my family has high blood pressure.’ That doesn't make untreated hypertension healthy. Likewise, widespread drinking doesn't eliminate the possibility that alcohol is causing harm."
Anyone experiencing symptoms of alcohol use disorder should consult a healthcare provider for evaluation and guidance.

title: Financial hardship may age the brain faster, researchers say in new study
summary: Chronic poverty over decades was linked to memory loss, slower processing speed and brain shrinkage, with strongest effects among men and APOE-ε4 carriers.
story: Sleep is critical for brain function and longevity, according to Dr. Daniel Amen, psychiatrist and owner of Amen Clinics in California.
Adults who faced persistent financial hardship showed poorer cognitive performance and signs of accelerated brain aging later in life, according to a new study.
Researchers at University College London looked at 2,759 U.K. participants from the MRC National Survey of Health and Development born in 1946, as stated in a press release.
Adults who reported experiencing persistent financial hardship or low income performed worse on cognitive tests that assessed verbal memory and processing speed.
LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS
Those who had persistent low income also showed poorer brain health based on MRI scans, which measured markers of aging like brain shrinkage and enlarged ventricles.

"[While] we know well that cognitive decline is associated with both genetic risks and adverse childhood experience, we knew very little about what happens during the life course — particularly, the experience of persistent financial stress over the lifetime," study author Dr. Jacques Wels from the Unit for Lifelong Health & Ageing at UCL told Fox News Digital.
Adults who faced persistent financial hardship showed poorer cognitive performance and signs of accelerated brain aging later in life, according to a new study. (iStock)
"The study clearly demonstrates … that the accumulation of poverty is linked to cognitive decline," Wels said.
"We used different measures of life course financial adversity and different measures of cognitive decline, and they all show the same results, which makes the results solid."
ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION
The associations were strongest among men, people who had disadvantaged childhoods and carriers of the APOE-ε4 genetic variant that is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer's disease.
Participants who reported experiencing persistent financial hardship or low income performed worse on cognitive tests that assessed verbal memory and processing speed. (iStock)

"The study shows that [while] cognitive decline is both a matter of genetic risks and individual behaviors, it is also affected by the experiences we live [throughout] our lives that we don’t always have control [over]," Wels added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Based on the findings, the researchers suggested that chronic financial adversity over decades, rather than short-term periods of hardship, is linked to faster cognitive aging.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
This could be the result of chronic stress leading to inflammation or increased cognitive load from persistent financial worry, the authors proposed.
There were some limitations of the study, including that its observational design could not prove that the financial stress caused the cognitive effects.
Those who had persistent low income also showed poorer brain health based on MRI scans, which measured markers of aging like brain shrinkage and enlarged ventricles. (iStock)

"We are looking at a cohort of people born in 1946 — so their life course experience is really dependent on the context they lived in," Wels noted. "For instance, we found stronger effects among males, which reflects the ‘breadwinner’ role of men in older cohorts, something we might not observe in more recent generations."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Even after accounting for many other factors that could influence brain health, it's still possible that unmeasured variables may have affected the results, the study authors acknowledged.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

While reducing long-term poverty could help protect brain health, the UCL team said further studies are needed to determine whether improving financial circumstances directly reduces the risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

title: Dad suffers heart attack days before daughter's wedding — then doctors make sure he walks her down the aisle
summary: Rick Nelson had a heart attack days before his daughter's wedding, but after a quadruple bypass, his care team moved the ceremony to the hospital rooftop.
story: Days before Rachel Nelson’s wedding to Dana Schultz, her dad, 61-year-old Rick Nelson, suffered a heart attack and had emergency quadruple bypass surgery.
A father who suffered a heart attack just days before his daughter's wedding refused to let open-heart surgery keep him from walking her down the aisle.

Days before the planned ceremony, Rick Nelson began having chest pains while at a friend’s home. His wife, Gail, rushed him to Cleveland Clinic’s Marymount Emergency Department, according to a hospital statement sent to Fox News Digital.

When it was confirmed that Nelson was having a heart attack, he was brought by helicopter to Cleveland Clinic's main campus. Doctors found multiple severe coronary blockages that would require open-heart surgery.
BRIDE IS WALKED DOWN WEDDING AISLE BY MAN WHO RECEIVED HER LATE FATHER'S HEART
As Nelson was prepped for surgery, he told his doctors, "My daughter, Rachel, is getting married Saturday. I have to be there."
Following a successful quadruple bypass performed by cardiothoracic surgeon Dr. Faisal Bakaeen, Nelson began recovering in the ICU.
A father who suffered a heart attack just days before his daughter's wedding refused to let open-heart surgery keep him from walking her down the aisle. (Camilla Florenca Photography)
The initial plan was for his daughter to come visit him the hospital so he could have a first look at her in her wedding dress — but that evolved into something much bigger.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Care teams from across the hospital worked together to make sure Nelson could take part in the June 6 wedding, coordinating every detail to safely move the ceremony to the hospital's rooftop.
Nelson gets a first look at his daughter in her wedding dress before accompanying her down the aisle. (Camilla Florenca Photography)

Just days after undergoing life-saving heart surgery, Nelson traded his hospital bed for a front-row seat at his daughter's wedding. His care team prepared the venue, helped Nelson get dressed for the occasion and made sure he was able to walk his daughter down the aisle.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Nearly 80 family members and friends gathered on the hospital rooftop, where caregivers lined the aisle as Nelson — still recovering from the surgery he’d undergone just days earlier — accompanied his daughter to meet her groom, Dana Schultz.
Rick Nelson is pictured with his daughter, Rachel, on her wedding day. (Camilla Florenca Photography)

"Moments like these remind us the work we do is about more than medicine. It’s about people, families and milestones that can’t be repeated — and the shared commitment of a team to make something so meaningful possible," said Dr. Bakaeen, according to Cleveland Clinic’s statement.
"It’s hard to put into words what this meant to us," Nelson’s wife said. "Everyone went above and beyond."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The celebration continued later that day at the couple’s reception, where the bride’s mother started her toast with a lighthearted quip: "He didn’t have to make this dramatic of a move to get out of giving a speech."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Nelson has since been discharged and is recovering at home with his family while beginning cardiac rehabilitation — grateful he was able to keep the promise he made to his daughter.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Skipping sleep may pack on pounds faster than you think, new study finds
summary: A Columbia University study found that losing just 90 minutes of sleep per night led to weight gain and larger waistlines in adults over six weeks.
story: During 'Fox & Friends' Wellness Week, sleep expert Dr. Rebecca Robbins analyzes popular sleep trends including melatonin, mouth taping, cooling pillows and sleep trackers. She explains melatonin's role in circadian rhythm, mouth taping benefits for nasal breathing and the importance of a 65-degree Fahrenheit sleep environment. Robbins advises adults aim for 7-9 hours of sleep per night for optimal health and longevity.
Regularly cutting back on sleep could cause the number on the scale to creep up, according to new research.

A study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that adults who got about 90 minutes less sleep each night for six weeks gained roughly one pound on average compared with periods when they got enough rest.

Researchers at Columbia University Irving Medical Center studied 95 adults who were already at risk for heart or metabolic disease, comparing six weeks of adequate sleep with six weeks of cutting about 90 minutes of sleep each night.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Regularly cutting back on sleep may cause the number on the scale to increase, a new study finds. (iStock)

By the end of the sleep-restricted phase, participants weighed about one pound more on average and had slightly larger waistlines. They also spent more time sitting, although their levels of moderate and vigorous exercise remained about the same.

While participants gained weight, researchers did not detect significant changes in body fat or muscle mass. They also did not track how much participants ate, so it's unclear what drove the increase.
Dr. Somi Javaid, an Ohio-based OB-GYN and founder of HerMD who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that sleep plays an important role in regulating the body's metabolism.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Javaid said chronic sleep deprivation can make it harder for the body to regulate weight, but noted that women going through menopause may be especially vulnerable because sleep problems become more common during that stage of life.
"We are destroying women's sleep at the exact life stage when their metabolism is [the] least able to absorb the hit, then telling them to eat less and exercise more," Javaid said.
Adults gained about one pound on average and had slightly larger waistlines after six weeks of restricted sleep, compared with periods when they got enough rest. (iStock)
She added that the American Heart Association now recognizes sleep as one of its "Life's Essential 8" for heart health and recommends adults get seven to nine hours of sleep each night.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Chronic short sleep is not a lifestyle quirk," Javaid said. "We need to treat sleep as a vital sign of health."
While the findings suggest regularly getting less sleep may contribute to weight gain, the researchers noted several limitations of the study.
Experts say menopause can make it even harder for women to regulate their weight because sleep problems often become more common. (iStock)
They said the six-week study may not have been long enough to detect meaningful changes in body fat, which can take longer to develop than changes in body weight.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The researchers also noted that the study's relatively small sample size limited their ability to compare results among different groups of participants. In addition, some hormone measurements were collected only in the morning and may not have reflected fluctuations that occur throughout the day.
Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Popular pastime sending more Americans to ER with devastating injuries
summary: Detroit-area doctors are reporting a spike in e-bike crash injuries as Class 3 bikes reaching 28 mph cause major trauma among inexperienced riders.
story: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is scrutinizing robotaxi safety, documenting multiple instances of autonomous vehicles driving into active emergency scenes and blocking first responders. NHTSA states an AV that cannot safely interact with first responders poses a danger to the public. They will meet with robotaxi developers this month to discuss solutions.
The Detroit, Michigan, metro area is reporting an uptick in serious incidents related to electric bikes (e-bikes).
Police are seeing a rise in e-bike crashes, while doctors say they're treating a growing number of related injuries, Fox 2 Detroit reported.
These incidents have reportedly led some communities to seek restrictions on e-bikes or to ban them altogether.
SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA
Some e-bikes can reach speeds of up to 28 miles per hour, increasing the potential severity of crashes on sidewalks and streets.
Fox 2 Detroit spoke with emergency room doctor Robert Sherwin of the Detroit Medical Center, who reported seeing everything from minor injuries to major trauma related to e-bike incidents.
Police are reportedly seeing a rise in e-bike crashes, while doctors say they're treating a growing number of related injuries. (iStock)
"These Class 3 bikes are probably more like motor vehicles," he said. "They travel up to 28 miles an hour, and a lot of riders aren't expecting that, might not be experienced in that."
"These e-bikes are heavier than regular bikes, and they travel much faster, but the human body doesn't change just because a bike has a motor."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Local bike shop owner John Hughes suggested the "real issue" has always been sharing the road with cars, Fox 2 Detroit also noted.
"Cars aren't looking out for bikes. ... People don't respect bikes as a form of transportation, and that's where it gets dangerous."
Hughes continued, "There's a ton of traffic out there. Everyone is on their cellphones. They're texting and driving constantly."
An e-bike rider told Fox 2 Detroit that e-biking is "way better than a car." (iStock)
E-bike rider Cam Cason told Fox 2 Detroit that he takes his e-bike to work and school, crediting it as a "very efficient way" to get around.
"Way better than a car, in my opinion," he said. "When you don't have to spend $30 or $40 just to get some gas, use the electric bike to get where you need to go."
TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME MAY TRIGGER LASTING BRAIN DELAYS, TOP HEALTH OFFICIAL WARNS
As concerns over e-bike safety grow nationwide, states are beginning to tighten regulations.
In New Jersey, a new law enacted this year requires e-bikes to be registered, and riders must be at least 15 years old and possess either a valid driver's license or an e-bike license to operate one.

The law was enacted amid growing concerns about e-bike crashes, including the death of a New Jersey teenager. Supporters argued that licensing, helmet and registration requirements would promote responsible riding and reduce bodily harm.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
NYU Langone Health released an advisory in April on the surge in brain and spine injuries related to e-bikes and scooters among riders and pedestrians in New York City.

A study published in the journal Neurosurgery found that medical emergencies involving pedal-powered and electric bikes and scooters accounted for nearly 7% of trauma patients admitted to NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue.
Trauma cases related to e-bikes seen in the emergency room increased from less than 10% in 2018 to more than 50% by 2023. (iStock)

One-third of the 914 patients treated for injuries involving pedal-powered and electric bikes and scooters suffered a traumatic brain injury. More than two-thirds required hospital admission and about 30% needed intensive care.

Physical harm linked to electric bikes and scooters increased from less than 10% of cases in 2018 to more than half by 2023, according to the study. The most common cause of injury, accounting for about half of all cases, was a collision with a car or truck.
"People don't respect bikes as a form of transportation, and that's where it gets dangerous."

Fewer than one-third of riders wore helmets, which was linked to a "significantly higher rate" of brain and facial injuries. The study found that 20% of patients tested positive for alcohol, which was associated with more severe head trauma and lower rates of helmet use.
Pedestrians struck by electric vehicles suffered brain injuries at nearly twice the rate of riders, according to an analysis of 69 pedestrian cases.
Pedestrians struck by electric vehicles suffered brain injuries at nearly double the rate of riders, researchers found. (iStock)

Corresponding author Hannah Weiss, M.D., a resident in the Department of Neurosurgery at NYU Grossman School of Medicine, commented in a statement that these findings suggest "micromobility injuries are producing serious brain and spinal trauma that demands neurosurgical care at a scale we haven’t seen before."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"In a busy urban setting, we are seeing more and more of these injuries firsthand," she went on. "The data point to actionable solutions – helmet use, safer bike lane design and enforcement — that could prevent many of these injuries and better protect both riders and pedestrians."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Paul P. Huang, M.D., associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and chief of neurosurgery at NYC Health + Hospitals/Bellevue, added that the study highlights that "urban infrastructure must continue to improve to keep pace with the rapid rise of electric bikes and scooters."

"Future studies should track these injuries across multiple cities and measure whether protected bike lanes, helmet programs and speed enforcement actually reduce the number of brain and spine surgeries we perform," Huang said.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Too much screen time may trigger lasting brain delays, top health official warns
summary: Federal health officials unveil "the 5 Ds" framework to help parents combat screen addiction and protect children's attention, memory and language skills.
story: Dr. Stephanie Haridopolos recommends creating a family screen plan, modeling healthy habits, redirecting kids to offline activities and disconnecting during meals, bedtime and car rides to build better connections.
As screens compete for families' attention, children's development is paying the price, top federal health officials warn.

Early and excessive screen time can trigger severe neurocognitive delays in young children, impacting attention spans, memory and language skills, according to Dr. Stephanie Haridopolos, interim surgeon general and principal deputy assistant secretary of health.
"Parents are now fighting for attention from the screens," Haridopolos told Fox News Digital.
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
To help parents combat screen addiction, the U.S. Surgeon General's Office has released a targeted framework known as "the 5 Ds."
No. 1: Discuss

Don't wait for a conflict to establish boundaries, experts recommend. Sit down as a family to outline clear, age-appropriate rules regarding when, where and how long screens can be used throughout the day.
Setting explicit expectations ahead of time cuts down on daily arguments, experts say.
High screen exposure in young children threatens early brain tissue development, leading to delays in attention, memory and speech, experts say. (iStock)
No. 2: Do (model the behavior)
Parents should model healthy screen habits themselves, Haridopolos said.
"If we're constantly on our screens, then perhaps our children will be, too," she said, encouraging adults to "be good role models and lead by example."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
No. 3: Divert

Rather than defaulting to giving children a tablet when they're bored, Haridopolos recommended steering them toward hands-on activities, such as doing arts and crafts or preparing a healthy meal together.
4. Disconnect
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Breaks like summer and the holidays are critical windows for families to reset digital boundaries, the interim surgeon general suggested.
Scrolling while eating can lead to higher caloric intake and increased consumption of ultraprocessed foods, the interim surgeon general warned. (iStock)
Haridopolos encouraged families to build regular screen-free periods into their daily routines, including during meals, car rides and before bedtime.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Mealtimes: Keep family dinners focused on face-to-face conversation.In the car: Treat travel time as a chance to reconnect rather than defaulting to phones or seat-back screens.Before bed: Turn off blue-light devices at least an hour before sleep to avoid disrupting natural sleep cycles.
Mealtimes: Keep family dinners focused on face-to-face conversation.
In the car: Treat travel time as a chance to reconnect rather than defaulting to phones or seat-back screens.
Before bed: Turn off blue-light devices at least an hour before sleep to avoid disrupting natural sleep cycles.
As part of the "Delay" step, the program recommended putting off children's access to screens whenever possible.  (iStock)
No. 5: Delay

As part of the "Delay" step, Haridopolos recommended putting off children's access to screens whenever possible. One way to do that, she said, is by requiring phones and other mobile devices to be charged overnight in a shared household space — like the kitchen or living room — rather than in children's bedrooms.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Those are some simple activities that you can do that will make huge changes in the future," the interim surgeon general added.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Man who beat rare cancer celebrates by canoeing 2,000 miles with his dog
summary: Frank Carter, 67, and his dog Amos completed a 2,000-mile canoe trip down the Missouri River four years after CAR T-cell therapy cleared his lymphoma.
story: Patient Laurie Adami credits the cancer treatment Car-T with saving her life on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

A 67-year-old cancer survivor from Orange County, Florida, completed a more than 2,000-mile journey down the Missouri River alongside his dog, Amos, after undergoing a groundbreaking immunotherapy treatment.
Frank Carter spent 64 days navigating the longest U.S. river in a cedar-strip canoe he built by hand, according to reports from the Moffitt Cancer Center and FOX 13 News.
The expedition began in Montana and concluded near St. Louis, Missouri, requiring the pair to camp along the riverbank while enduring severe storms, high winds and hail, FOX 13 News reported.
'FIT MOM' DID 'EVERYTHING RIGHT' — THEN A COLON CANCER DIAGNOSIS CHANGED HER LIFE

Before his diagnosis, Carter was a long-distance adventurer. According to the Moffitt Cancer Center, he spent five months hiking the Appalachian Trail in 2019 and completed an eight-week cross-country bicycle ride from San Diego to New Smyrna Beach, Florida, in 2020.
However, his physical limits were tested in a new way in 2021 after a routine 5K race.
Frank Carter, a 67-year-old cancer survivor from Orange County, Fla., paddled 2,341 miles down the Missouri River over 64 days with his golden retriever, Amos. (UCG/Universal Images Group via G)
"I was wiped out. I just wasn't recovering," Carter told FOX 13 News. "I went to my doctor, had blood tests. Long story short, in two weeks I was getting chemo."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Doctors diagnosed Carter with mantle cell lymphoma, a rare form of blood cancer that originates in white blood cells known as lymphocytes. He underwent 15 rounds of chemotherapy in Orlando, according to Moffitt Cancer Center.
Carter hand-built the cedar-strip canoe (not pictured) for the journey, and is now sharing his story to encourage other patients to remain active and hopeful. (iStock)
Although the treatment significantly reduced the cancer, follow-up exams showed lingering traces of the disease.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Carter then sought care at the Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa to undergo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, which involves extracting the patient's own immune cells, genetically altering them in a laboratory to identify cancer cells, and adding them back into the body.
Doctors treated Carter with CAR T-cell therapy, a groundbreaking immunotherapy that genetically alters a patient's own T-cells to attack cancer, leaving him cancer-free for four years. (iStock)

"We take those T-cells and genetically engineer them by putting something called a CAR into them," Dr. Michael Jain, an oncologist at Moffitt Cancer Center, told FOX 13 News. "Now these T-cells can see the tumor and get rid of it, where before the tumor was able to hide from it."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Carter has remained cancer-free for four years after the single infusion. Throughout his recovery, he has found constant support in his dog, Amos, whom he brought home right before beginning chemotherapy.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"After my cancer diagnosis, I told myself I was going to beat this, and I really wanted a dog during the process," Carter told Moffitt's Endeavor publication. "I got Amos right before my first treatment."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Longer lives, worse health? Scientists uncover troubling trend across generations
summary: The morbidity gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy is widest in America, where people spend about 14 years in poor health.
story: Rates of chronic disease, obesity and stress continue to rise across America. Experts warn that some of the healthiest habits from the nation's earlier centuries may have fallen by the wayside.
People across the world are living longer, but they’re also spending more years coping with ill health, a recent study observed.

The "morbidity gap" — the number of years people spend in poor health, typically struggling with chronic challenges such as low back pain, hearing loss and depression — widened across 203 of 204 countries analyzed and was the most pronounced in America, the researchers found.

"Globally in 2023, an average of 14.5% of life was spent in poor health, compared to 13.6% in 1990," the researchers at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington reported.
JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'
In the United States, the morbidity gap is about 14 years, or 17.8% of the expected lifespan.

"Between 1990 and 2023, global life expectancy at birth increased from 64.6 years to 73.8 years, while healthy life expectancy rose from 55.9 years to 63.1 years," the researchers reported in a news release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
"Because gains in survival consistently outpaced gains in healthy years of life, people are spending more years living with chronic disease and disability."
A recent study found that the number of years people spend in poor health is widening, especially in America. (iStock)

The gap widened the most in the wealthiest countries where populations have access to life-extending resources, the researchers reported. Women are also living longer than men but are also spending more years in poor health, they found.

"To me, the most important message of this study is not that people are living longer. It is that we have become far better at delaying death than delaying functional decline," Dr. Antony Chu, clinical assistant professor at Brown University’s Warren Alpert School of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.

"Modern medicine has achieved remarkable success in reducing mortality from cardiovascular disease, cancer, trauma and infectious illness," he added. "Yet many of those additional years are now lived with chronic pain, disability, sensory loss, depression or reduced independence."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers analyzed Global Burden of Disease data covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 through 2023. In their report, published by The Lancet Public Health, scientists observed that a small number of chronic, largely non-fatal causes were the primary contributors to the morbidity gap.

Musculoskeletal disorders, especially low back pain; mental disorders, such as depression and anxiety; hearing loss, falls and other non-communicable accounted for about 57% of all years lived in poor health worldwide. High fasting plasma glucose, obesity and aging populations were also important contributors.
The researchers noted that the study points to broad health trends but doesn’t prove exactly what's causing people to spend more years in poor health.
Researchers recently found people are spending more years living with chronic diseases and disabilities. (iStock)

"Our findings suggest that future gains in population health will come not only from helping people live longer, but from helping them live healthier," said Dr. Christopher Murray, director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington School of Medicine and senior author of the study.

"Progress in healthy aging should be measured not only by lifespan, but by healthspan [the number of years spent in good health], with greater investment in prevention, long-term disease management and chronic care to reduce years lived in poor health."

The goal should no longer be simply extending lifespan, but compressing morbidity and maximizing the number of years people remain physically, cognitively and socially well, Chu told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Ultimately, I believe the next frontier of medicine is not simply adding years to life, but adding life to years," he said. "First, we need to focus on preserving function rather than simply reacting to disease."

The approach involves routinely assessing mobility, muscle strength, balance, hearing, cognition and overall physical resilience. Chu said this may prove just as important as monitoring blood pressure, cholesterol and glucose.
"Functional decline often begins years before disability becomes obvious, providing an opportunity for earlier intervention," he said.
Many older Americans are socially isolated, though research shows relationships are important to longevity, an expert said. (iStock)
Musculoskeletal health also deserves much greater emphasis, Chu said.

"Progressive resistance training, fall prevention, maintenance of muscle mass and early treatment of chronic back pain should become core components of preventive medicine rather than afterthoughts," he said. "Preserving mobility may ultimately have as much impact on healthy aging as preventing heart disease."
Mental health and social connection are another vital component to healthspan, Chu said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Hearing loss, depression, anxiety and loneliness frequently reinforce one another, accelerating physical decline while diminishing quality of life," he said. "Addressing these conditions early may improve both longevity and independence."
Chu, who is the child of immigrants, said it’s his belief that Americans often overlook an important cultural dimension of healthy aging.

"In many societies outside the United States, older adults continue to play an active and respected role within multigenerational families," he said. "They remain mentors, caregivers, historians and sources of wisdom. This continued sense of purpose and belonging may provide meaningful protection against loneliness, depression and loss of identity.
A continued sense of purpose and belonging may lead people to live longer and healthier lives, according to an expert. (iStock)

"By contrast, many older Americans experience increasing social isolation precisely when maintaining meaningful relationships may be most important," Chu added. "Healthy aging is not determined solely by biology; it is also shaped by community, purpose and human connection."
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: 'Fit Mom' did 'everything right' — then a colon cancer diagnosis changed her life
summary: Maria Kang, the viral "No Excuses Mom" fitness influencer, reveals how Stage 4 colon cancer blindsided her despite years of healthy living.
story: Maria Kang told Fox News Digital she thought healthy eating and regular exercise would protect her until a Stage 4 colon cancer diagnosis revealed a different reality.

Maria Kang built her career around fitness, healthy eating and helping other moms prioritize wellness. Despite believing she had done "everything right," the California mother of three was blindsided by colon cancer.
Kang, now 46, said the diagnosis reshaped her understanding of what it means to be healthy.
She became an internet sensation in 2013 after a photo of her sculpted physique alongside her three young sons sparked a global conversation about fitness and motherhood.
LEADING ONCOLOGIST REVEALS 6 HABITS THAT COULD PROMOTE LONGEVITY AND REDUCE YOUR RISK OF CHRONIC ILLNESS
The viral image — captioned "What’s your excuse?" — led to her being dubbed the "No Excuse Mom" and inspired the launch of hundreds of wellness communities around the world.
More than a decade later, Kang’s world was turned upside down when she learned that she had Stage 4 colon cancer in November 2023.
Maria Kang built her career around fitness, healthy eating and helping other moms prioritize wellness but then was blindsided by colon cancer. (Beth Baugher, Maria Kang)

"It was definitely a complete shock because I was the healthiest person I knew," she shared with Fox News Digital. "I wanted to blame the food, but I didn't eat bad food. I filtered my water. There was no excuse why I had this cancer."
Looking back, Kang said she had experienced persistent digestive problems since adolescence, including chronic constipation and bloating that worsened with stress.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
"It didn't matter how many fiber pills or laxatives, it just took a long time to go," she said. "So, that's been an ongoing journey throughout my life."
Over the years, Kang said, she convinced herself that her digestive problems were just something she had to live with.
Kang became an internet sensation in 2013 after a photo of her sculpted physique alongside her three young sons sparked a global conversation about fitness and motherhood. (Mike Byerly)

"One thing that I realized is that we normalize problems, and we think it's OK, but it’s not OK," she said. "Digestion should be like breathing. It should be like inhaling and exhaling. It should be simple. But it wasn't simple."

After a tumor was detected through a biopsy after a colonoscopy, Kang said she initially pursued holistic approaches for 12 weeks, but the tumor did not shrink and may have grown slightly. She then began FOLFOX, a combination of chemotherapy drugs used to treat some gastrointestinal cancers, in 2024.
MELINDA FRENCH GATES SAYS IT TOOK 3 DOCTORS TO DIAGNOSE THE CONDITION SHE WAS SUFFERING FROM

After one treatment, Kang went to the emergency room when her colostomy stoma retracted, and a scan reportedly showed that the tumor had shrunk substantially. She then asked to stop chemotherapy and proceed with surgery.

Kang later underwent extensive surgery to remove the tumor and about a foot of her colon, along with multiple reproductive organs and her appendix. She temporarily required a colostomy and later an ileostomy.
"It was definitely a complete shock because I was the healthiest person I knew."
Today, Kang says her MRIs have shown "no suspicious mass detected." She gets regular blood screenings and scans every six months.

"Much of what remains appears related to postoperative healing and inflammation," she shared. "Because of my history, my doctors continue surveillance, but I have not been formally declared NED (no evidence of disease)."
Alarming trends
An estimated 158,850 Americans will be diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2026, and around 55,230 people will die from the disease this year, according to the American Cancer Society.

Although colorectal cancer incidence has declined overall — largely among older adults, a trend linked in part to increased screening and changes in certain risk factors — rates are rising in younger age groups.
Kang said her fitness and nutrition regimens also look drastically different from her pre-cancer routines. (Maria Kang)
Among adults younger than 50, colorectal cancer incidence increased by 2.9% per year from 2013 to 2022.

The American Cancer Society and U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommend that people at average risk begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45, although those with certain risk factors may need to start earlier.
Anyone experiencing persistent or concerning symptoms should consult a doctor, regardless of age.
‘I look healthy’
"It was a really big, humbling look in the mirror when you say to yourself, 'I look healthy, but I'm not healthy,’" Kang told Fox News Digital.
"When someone is at a normal range in their weight, they could have cancer. They could have autoimmune issues.
DOCTORS PUSH NEW BLOOD TESTS FOR COLON CANCER AS CASES SURGE IN YOUNGER ADULTS
"We don't know what's going on inside of a person. We always just want to look the part versus be the part."
Wellness redefined
Kang said her cancer journey has changed her perception of health and what’s important in life.

"Cancer makes everything extremely clear — what's important, what is not important, what you should eat, what you shouldn't eat," she said. "If you really listen to yourself, it becomes crystal clear when you have no energy."
Kang’s world was turned upside down when she learned that she had Stage 4 colon cancer in November 2023. (Maria Kang)
Kang said her fitness and nutrition regimens also look drastically different from her pre-cancer routines.

"I used to train five or six days a week, but now I only move when I want to," she said. "Walking is my best friend. I love to dance. I still love to strength-train because it's fun for me and it makes me strong."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Perhaps the biggest shift is that Kang no longer does anything that feels forced.
"If there's anything that I feel forced to do, I don't do it," she said. "If I feel awful, my body's going to express awful."
Her approach to food has also shifted, she shared.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"In the past, there were bad foods and good foods and cheat days … what I understand now is balance," Kang said.
While she does naturally veer toward fruits and vegetables — "things that have water and life and light in them" — Kang said she is still open to eating any other foods, including pizza.
Kang underwent extensive surgery to remove the tumor and about a foot of her colon, along with multiple reproductive organs and her appendix. (Maria Kang)
Overall, Kang wants people to know that maintaining healthy habits does not eliminate the possibility of developing cancer.
"It could happen to anybody. That was the most humbling realization," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"You may think you're young and healthy and this won't happen to you, but this world is so unpredictable right now. Anything can happen to anybody.
"Health is not what you think it is," she said. "It's not just how you look. It's how you feel."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The American Cancer Society recommends seeing a healthcare provider about persistent changes in bowel habits, blood in the stool, abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss or other concerning gastrointestinal symptoms.
While such symptoms can have many causes other than cancer, they should be evaluated regardless of a person’s age.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Bombshell voting scandal adds to pattern of noncitizen voters as Trump warns of threat to ‘heart' of democracy
summary: A 25-year record of state reviews and software failures reveals noncitizens on voter rolls across multiple states, but no federal law compels reporting.
story: America First Legal President Gene Hamilton posits that there are ways to fix ongoing problems with U.S. voting systems.

New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s recent announcement of 6,600 ineligible voters found on the state’s rolls is only the latest in a decades-long string of cases involving noncitizens registered to vote in U.S. elections, records show.

Sherrill said that the ineligible voters were registered due to a "serious software error" in New Jersey’s Motor Vehicle System. Her announcement came within a week of a major address from President Donald Trump in which he warned that digital election interference posed a "cyber threat aimed at the very heart of our democracy."

While New Jersey is the latest documented failure, it is not an isolated anomaly. New Jersey's error adds to a 25-year record of state reviews, software failures and prosecutions that found noncitizens on voter rolls and, in some documented cases, casting ballots. Experts say the episodes establish a recurring vulnerability. However, due to the lack of a national standard for identifying and reporting errors, reviews are sporadic and use different methods, making it impossible to determine how widespread the problem truly is.

"It's a major vulnerability," Jason Snead, executive director of the conservative think tank the Honest Elections Project, told Fox News Digital. "And we have seen just within the last couple of years many states that have checked their voter rolls and found non-citizens on them … So, this is a big problem."
NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION

Mikie Sherrill, governor of New Jersey, speaks in the Assembly Chamber of the New Jersey State House in Trenton, New Jersey, US, on Tuesday, March 10, 2026. (Heather Khalifa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

According to New Jersey’s preliminary findings, fewer than 400 individuals who were improperly registered ended up voting. Sherrill said they lived all across the state and mostly lacked a party affiliation, though there were some registered as Democrats or Republicans.

Fox News Digital reached out to the New Jersey Secretary of State Division of Elections, state Attorney General Dale Caldwell and the chairs of several key legislative elections oversight committees for clarification on which elections the 400 ineligible voters participated in and to request details on the state’s auditing protocols. Fox News Digital did not receive a response from any of the state officials mentioned above.

Snead explained that though states are required by law to ensure their voter rolls are up to date and accurate, there is no uniform federal requirement for a state to disclose its findings. He said that this has led to differences across states in how the law is enforced and how errors are reported.

"There are federal requirements to maintain clean and accurate voter rolls. And of course, it is a federal crime for a noncitizen to register and to vote, but there's no requirement that a state report how many non-citizens that they have found up to the federal government. That's entirely a state law question," he explained.
He argued that problems involving noncitizen voting are greater in blue states due to policies he said make it easier to cheat.
LEAVITT RIPS BLUE STATE’S EXPLOSIVE NONCITIZEN VOTER-ROLL ADMISSION: ‘NOT A COINCIDENCE’

"When you look at the policies that are pushed in blue states by the left, things like automatic voter registration, giving drivers licenses to illegal aliens, banning voter identification laws, no proof of citizenship to vote on and on and, this is the inevitable outcome of all of those policies," said Snead, adding, "This is not the first time that we've seen a state with automatic voter registration add potential non-citizens to the rolls."

After the president’s speech, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin released a statement announcing that preliminary DHS reviews of state records found "as many as" 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in four states: 35,152 in New Jersey, 190,832 in California, 15,903 in Nevada and 14,576 in Pennsylvania.

Fox News Digital reached out to DHS for clarification on its preliminary findings. However, DHS did not answer Fox News Digital’s questions and instead sent a statement from Mullin reiterating the number.

In the statement, Mullin emphasized to Fox News Digital that "this shouldn’t be a red or blue state issue: ONLY Americans should elect American leaders." He added that "we’ve put these governors on notice. States must work with us to ensure free, fair, and honest elections."

Charles Stewart III, a professor of political science specializing in elections at MIT, explained that the controlling federal law governing voter registration, the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), is "silent on the issue of noncitizens on the roll."

He told Fox News Digital that because "this was not an issue in the early 1990s … one of the ambiguities right now and controversies is over precisely what sort of obligations states have to audit their rolls for noncitizens."

"This is really at the crux of the matter and two of President Trump's executive orders. It's the crux of the matter in the Save America Act. It is the crux to the matter in the current efforts, well, back to the executive orders and a lot of the lawsuits. And the states are pointing out, when being pressed by the federal government, that yes, it is illegal for noncitizens to vote, for sure, and states should have an obligation to make sure noncitizens are not registering, but there is no federal law that compels states to do investigations, nor is there a federal law to compel them to report.

Meanwhile, states that have published review results have reported concerning findings. Besides New Jersey, state reviews conducted since 2020 have found evidence of significant numbers of noncitizens registered to vote in Louisiana, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio and Illinois, a Fox News Digital review found.

Earlier this year, Louisiana Secretary of State said that using the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database, which was rolled out by the Trump administration last year, the state identified 403 noncitizens on its voter rolls, 83 of whom had voted in elections, American Press reported.

In 2025, an audit by the Iowa secretary of state confirmed that 277 noncitizens were registered to vote and that 35 successfully voted in the 2024 election while five attempted to vote but were rejected.
TRUMP RELEASES DECLASSIFIED ELECTION INTELLIGENCE, SAYS IT REVEALS 'SHOCKING VULNERABILITIES'

The same year, the Michigan Department of State published its findings from a review of the 2024 election, which it said proved that "credible cases of noncitizens casting a ballot in Michigan elections are extremely rare." The review found that 15 people, who it said "appear to be non-U.S. citizens," cast a ballot in the election. Additionally, the department identified a Chinese national who allegedly voted illegally.

The Ohio Secretary of State's Office announced in 2024 and 2021 that it had identified 597 and 117 apparent noncitizen voter registrations, respectively, and referred the cases for further investigation.

According to findings cited in Illinois legislation and testimony by secretary of state officials before the general assembly, a programming error in the state's automatic voter registration system allowed the records of 574 people who identified themselves as noncitizens to be transmitted to election officials between 2018 and 2019.
Further, officials in Pennsylvania, Texas, Maryland, Colorado, Florida and North Carolina have also reported cases of noncitizens being registered to vote as far back as 2000.

In testimony given to the Pennsylvania House State Government Committee in 2017, then elections commissioner Jonathan Marks revealed that the state had found 1,160 records of apparent noncitizens who self-reported and canceled. Marks said that a deeper analysis of the years 2000 through 2017 found 544 ballots were cast by the identified registrants.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
In Texas, authorities discovered a resident alien named Rosa Ortega registered in 2002 and voted five times from 2004 through 2014, according to Attorney General Ken Paxton.

In another case, a Ghanaian national named Michael Nana Baako registered to vote in Maryland, swearing that he was a U.S. citizen in 2005 and subsequently voted in 10 federal elections between 2006 and 2018, according to the DOJ.

A 2012 report by the Colorado Department of State revealed that the state identified 3,903 registered voters whose citizenship status was "in question." An additional 430 Colorado voters were found to have identified themselves as ineligible to vote because of citizenship requirements.

The report noted that in Colorado "no proof is required to validate the status indicated on a registration form." It said that individuals can register to vote at a driver’s license office, state public assistance office, county office, private voter registration drive, or even online, none of which verify citizenship.
Three reviews conducted by the Florida Department of State for the years between 2013 and 2017 identified 821 noncitizen registrations and 126 people with voting histories.
Meanwhile, a 2017 state audit in North Carolina concluded that 41 legal-status noncitizens cast ballots.
NJ REPUBLICAN SAYS MOTOR VOTER SCANDAL VINDICATES YEARS OF ELECTION INTEGRITY WARNINGS, PUSHES FOR LEGISLATIVE PROBE
(Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images) (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital also reached out to the Justice Department to ask how many individuals the agency has charged with noncitizen voting or unlawful voter registration since 2000. However, a spokesperson for the DOJ did not offer specifics. Instead, the spokesperson sent Fox News Digital a statement assuring that the department’s Civil Rights Division "is investigating and will keep pressing states to clean their rolls" and is "prosecuting cases where the law and evidence support it."
The DOJ spokesperson reiterated that "it is illegal for any noncitizen to vote in a federal election" and that "every unlawful vote dilutes the voice of American citizens."

"Whether or not a case is prosecutable doesn't change the fact that the wrongful vote happened — DHS found over 250,000 likely noncitizens on voter rolls nationwide, and New Jersey's own Governor confirmed 400 noncitizens voted there," the spokesperson said.
"The fact of the matter is that election after election after election after election happened and no one did anything about it," remarked Gene Hamilton, president of America First Legal.

He pointed to a letter sent by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division to election officials in all 50 states which he said, "reminded them of their obligations and the possibility of legal consequences for not taking action."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Since President Donald Trump's return to office, the Civil Rights Division has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking to compel the production of full voter registration lists under the NVRA, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.
"There are ways to fix it," said Hamilton. "It's just a matter of desire."
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Moreno unloads on Fauci after Senate hearing, calls him Democrats' 'hero' over pandemic policies
summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno says Anthony Fauci is Democrats' "hero" who "treated us like lab rats" after Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment during a Senate hearing on COVID-19 policies.
story: Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, reflects on Dr. Anthony Fauci’s testimony on ‘Hannity.’

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, doubled down Thursday on his criticism of Dr. Anthony Fauci after the former top health official declined to answer questions during a Senate hearing, calling him Democrats' "hero."
Appearing on "Hannity" Thursday evening, Moreno argued Fauci's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic was driven by a desire for power rather than public health.
"This is about controlling American people," Moreno said. "He treated us like lab rats."
Moreno said Fauci's approach to the pandemic reflected what he believes Democrats ultimately want from government.
TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, criticized Dr. Anthony Fauci's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity." (Anna Moneymaker / Getty Images)

"You want to give power to Democrats, socialists and communists in this country? They will take away your freedoms, they will take away your liberties, they'll control you, they'll replace you," he said. "They want to systematically destroy this country, and that's why Fauci is their hero. He got to do what they only fantasize about, which is total and complete control of the American people."

Moreno and Fauci clashed during Wednesday's Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing after Fauci, on the advice of counsel, invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and declined to answer questions from committee members.
RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. Fauci was expected to be questioned about his diary entries during his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. (Getty Images)
A frustrated Moreno told Fauci that the former White House chief medical advisor had inspired him to run for the Senate because of his influence over COVID-19 policies.
"Here I am sitting in front of you six years later saying, 'Who the f--- do you think you were for doing that? It is a total disgrace what you did to this country,'" Moreno said.
Asked Thursday whether he stood by those remarks, Moreno argued Fauci's influence set back children's health for decades and devastated small businesses.
"The reality is this guy damaged a lot of things in this country," he said.
FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Senator Bernie Moreno, a Republican from Ohio, during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, DC on Wednesday, June 17. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Moreno also pointed to more than 1,000 pages of internal notes released by committee Chairman Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., ahead of the hearing. According to Paul, the notes suggest Fauci privately expressed views about COVID-19 that differed from some of his public statements.
"This is one of the most depraved bureaucrats," Moreno said, adding that Fauci should face prosecution over his handling of the pandemic.

Although Fauci received a pardon from former President Joe Biden, Moreno noted that state investigations remain possible. On Thursday, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced his office would open an investigation after Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right during Wednesday's hearing.

"We know what he was actually thinking," Moreno said. "We know he lied to the American people. State attorneys general, like the one in Florida—I hope the one in Ohio does the same thing. We got to pursue this guy."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci listens during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Fauci declined to answer questions, asserting his Fifth Amendment right. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Moreno said the moment that bothered him most during the hearing came when he asked Fauci to apologize to audience members who said they were harmed by or disagreed with pandemic policies.
"He wouldn't even look at them," Moreno said. "That's how despicable this guy is."
Fox News Digital's Alex Miller, Adam Pack and Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.
Fox News Digital has reached out to Fauci's attorney for comment.
