How to shop for jelly shoes that won’t hurt your feet
If you want to try the jelly trend, Landau suggests prioritizing the following things when you are shopping to ensure they are as comfortable as possible.

Support: Look for a pair with at least some built-in arch support or a contoured footbed rather than a completely flat sole. This will keep your feet (and body) aligned and feeling good as you wear them. It depends on who you ask — and which pair you’re wearing. Plenty of shoppers rave about how surprisingly comfortable certain jelly shoes are, especially ones with a cushioned footbed or a bit of give in the material. But comfort with jelly shoes tends to be more inconsistent than with traditional footwear, since the rigid plastic construction doesn’t mold to your foot the way leather or canvas does.

Some people find they can wear a pair for longer stretches with no issues, while others deal with rubbing, blisters or foot fatigue after just a few hours. If you’re going to try the trend, look for details like a contoured or padded insole, some flexibility in the material, and a roomy toe box — those features tend to make the biggest difference in how comfortable a jelly shoe actually feels on your foot, according to Landau.

If you’re set on wearing jelly shoes but worried about blisters, there are a few ways to add some protection before they become a problem. “You can apply silicone band-aids to the posterior heel or moleskin as well to create a buffer to the shear forces to prevent skin irritation and rubbing,” says Landau. Applying these to any spot on your foot that tends to rub — like the back of your heel or the sides of your toes — before you put your shoes on can help prevent friction from ever turning into a blister in the first place.

title: Seattle police chief resigns days after food festival shooting
summary: A reason for Chief Shon Barnes’ resignation wasn’t disclosed. There have been questions this week over the release of information about the shooting Sunday, which killed two bystanders.
story: Seattle’s police chief resigned Thursday after days of questions about the release of information following a shooting at a food festival that left three people dead, including two bystanders.
Mayor Katie Wilson accepted a letter of resignation from Police Chief Shon Barnes, she said in a statement released by the police department. The statement does not say why Barnes resigned.
Wilson told NBC affiliate KING of Seattle that “multiple factors” led to the change.
“I’ll say that this decision was not solely due to the events of Sunday,” she told the station. “Multiple factors figured into this decision and into the conversation that the chief and I had.”

Barnes, whom the previous mayor appointed to head the department in 2024, was questioned along with Wilson about initial reports that two suspects had been arrested after Sunday’s violence at the Bite of Seattle event, when only one had been arrested.
“We understand that people are angry. You should be. Everyone should be angry,” Barnes said at a news conference Monday.
There were also questions about a five-hour delay in the official release of more information in the wake of the shooting, which occurred around 6 p.m. Sunday.

“We want to get out information as early and as often as possible. It is unfortunate that sometimes in any situation, early information is sometimes incorrect,” Barnes said then. He said the department would look at how to do better in the future.
Deputy Chief Andre Sayles was named interim police chief, the statement about the resignation said.
Wilson said in Thursday’s statement that “Chief Barnes has served this department and this city with dedication, and I am grateful for his service.”
Barnes said, “It has been an honor to serve the Seattle Police Department and this city.”
City Council President Joy Hollingsworth and council members Dan Strauss, Debora Juarez and Bob Kettle criticized the move as rash.

“Having cycled through four police chiefs in just two and a half years, our priority must be stability, not further disruption,” they said in a joint statement. “The people of Seattle deserve reliable leadership, especially as we close out a busy summer of public events.”
Barnes was the second Black police chief of Seattle. He previously was chief of the Madison, Wisconsin, Police Department.
Several Black community organizations, including the Seattle NAACP and the Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle, urged the mayor in a letter earlier Thursday not to remove Barnes.

“The tragic fatal shooting at the Bite of Seattle was heartbreaking for our city, but Chief Barnes should not be made a scapegoat for the complex challenges of public safety,” the letter said, calling it “the wrong decision at the wrong time.”

Barnes has faced criticism for spending time in Chicago, where his family lives. Sgt. Patrick Michaud, a police spokesperson, said Thursday that Barnes has made four trips to Chicago this year and spent about 18 days in total traveling there. Barnes also has traveled to several police executive and recruitment conferences. Barnes said Monday that he had been in Dallas for the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement Executives conference when the shooting occurred.
The Seattle Police Officers Guild, a union that has clashed with Wilson, criticized Wilson’s administration for what it called “confusion, mixed messages, and chaos surrounding Chief Barnes.”
“Seattle doesn’t need another week of political drama. It needs leadership,” union President Kent Loux said.
Three people in all were killed in Sunday’s gunfire, police said: two bystanders and a 19-year-old who was one of the shooters. Four others were injured.
Police continued to look for a third possible shooter Thursday.

Police arrested a 15-year-old suspect shortly after Sunday’s shooting, and they have called the 19-year-old who was killed an associate of that teenager. Police said in court documents that the arrested 15-year-old said “love you bro” as he passed the fatally shot 19-year-old.
Bystanders were killed and injured and crowds ran from the gunfire at the annual three-day event at Seattle Center, the same complex as the city’s famous Space Needle, officials said.
Prosecutors have charged the 15-year-old with one count each of first-degree assault with a firearm enhancement and second-degree unlawful possession of a firearm.

Police said in court documents that the 15-year-old had a 9 mm handgun in his coat when he was arrested and that police saw him firing multiple times. The document described the gun as a Polymer80 firearm, which is sold in parts and assembled by the user.
But preliminary test results from that handgun appear to exclude it as the gun responsible for the deaths, police said in the court document, a probable cause statement filed Wednesday.
Thirteen shell casings have been recovered, and investigators believe there were four handguns, police said in the document.
Most were 9 mm, and four were .40-caliber, it said.

title: Teen girl kidnapped in Chicago is found alive in Virginia after being held captive for 4 years
summary: The case involves a 15-year-old girl who left home in Milwaukee, came to Chicago and then vanished. She was found alive in Virginia, and a man has been charged with kidnapping.
story: CHICAGO — A shocking update has ended the mystery of a missing child and kidnapping case, as a teenager who disappeared from Chicago has been found four years later in Virginia, having been held captive all this time, according to NBC 5 Investigates.

The alleged kidnapping happened outside a Chicago movie theater on June 23, 2022, according to law enforcement. The 15-year-old girl had taken an Uber from Milwaukee to Chicago to meet a man who had arranged the ride for her, authorities said. She had been communicating with the man online for several years, they said.
Investigators said the man convinced the teen to meet up, and he held her captive ever since that day.
“Her dad called me and was like, ‘Her phone’s going to voicemail.’ I knew immediately it was just off.”
The parents of Joniah Walker, now 19, said they knew a switched-off cellphone was the key clue that their daughter was in danger.

The teenager became a well-publicized missing person, her family and friends begging for help and criticizing Milwaukee police for moving too slowly. They went on local TV, pointing to a doorbell camera video of the last time the teenager was seen as evidence of a sloppy investigation.
“Why didn’t the police go knock on people’s doors? Like everybody on that block has a Ring camera. We got the videos, not the police,” one relative said.
“No one interviewed me; no one sat me down. It was us versus the police stations with a glass between us,” stated another.
Four years later, Walker was found 730 miles away, in a small frame home in Blacksburg, Virginia.

Police said she was sexually and physically abused while being held as a captive by 37-year-old Owen Anderson. Records state the man disposed of her cellphone — and a burner phone he’d sent her to use — in a sidewalk trash can.
A few days ago, Milwaukee County authorities filed kidnapping and child abduction charges against Anderson, who has yet to appear in Wisconsin court and is still in custody in Virginia.

Milwaukee police declined NBC 5 Investigates’ request to discuss the alleged kidnapping or answer questions about the investigation. An officer on the case had previously said they had no indication the teenager had been targeted by an organized abduction ring.
“I can assure you we have no reason to believe that she was involved in human trafficking,” Milwaukee Police Officer Jamie Sromalla told NBC affiliate WTMJ of Milwaukee in 2025.

In an email to NBC Chicago on Wednesday, a Milwaukee police official reiterated that position, saying that it would be misleading to report the teenage girl had been a victim of human trafficking. However, the charges clearly lay out that authorities say she was the victim of a kidnapping, child abduction and sexual abuse while being held against her will for years.
If you are a child being abused or know a child who may be facing abuse, call the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at (800) 422-4453 or go to childhelphotline.org.

title: Nursing mother of two and asylum-seeker detained by ICE in Tennessee
summary: The woman, who advocates said fled “extreme domestic violence” in Guatemala, has a 10-month-old baby and a 2-year-old with Down syndrome.
story: A nursing mother and Guatemalan asylum-seeker who was preparing to take her two young children to the doctor was arrested by ICE in Tennessee and is now being detained nearly 700 miles away from her family, according to advocacy groups that filed a civil rights complaint on her behalf.

The woman, who is referred to by the pseudonym Maria Pérez, fled “extreme domestic violence” in Guatemala and was seeking asylum in the U.S. when she was arrested in Nashville in May, said Katie Blankenship, the founder and managing attorney of Sanctuary of the South, an immigration and LGBTQ civil rights cooperative. Pérez is using a pseudonym out of fear of immigration retaliation.
Pérez has a 10-month-old baby, whom she had been nursing when she was arrested, and a 2-year-old with Down syndrome. She does not have a criminal history, advocates said.
“A mother getting her children into car seats to go to a doctor’s appointment is just ripped away from her children,” she said. “It’s just living an absolute nightmare. It’s a mother’s worst fear.”

The advocacy group, along with the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition, filed a complaint calling for Pérez’s immediate release with the Depart of Homeland Security’s Office of the Inspector General and other agencies Wednesday. The complaint is supported by the ACLU of Louisiana, the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and Amnesty International.
Since pe’s detention, “her daughters have been in the care of a neighbor, as the family has no other support network in the area,” according to the complaint.

The civil rights complaint said Pérez was detained in violation of a policy directive that says ICE should not detain or arrest people who are known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing unless there are exceptional circumstances, such as that they are national security risks or pose a danger.

“ICE and DHS continue to show blatant disregard not just for their own policies but for basic humanity,” Spring Miller, the senior director of legal strategy at the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition, said in a statement.
The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement Thursday evening that “pregnant and nursing women in ICE detention are exceedingly rare.”

“When this occurs, the women receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support, and accommodations aligned with community standards of care,” a DHS spokesperson said. The spokesperson did not say why Pérez detained.

The Trump administration has not revoked the policy, but advocates have said that as arrests and detention have surged overall, they have seen an increase in the number of pregnant, nursing and postpartum women in detention facilities.
On May 19, ICE agents arrived at Pérez’s home seeking the father of her children, who is separately facing federal charges, according to the complaint.

Pérez “was not named in any warrant and was not the subject of the enforcement action, but was nonetheless taken into ICE custody while putting her daughters in the car and preparing to go to a medical appointment,” the complaint said.

She was taken into custody in Tennessee, before being transferred days later to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana, a jurisdiction that does not allow bond for people who entered the country illegally, Blankenship said.

DHS said in its statement that Pérez was detained while ICE was serving a federal warrant at her residence in Nashville and that she previously faced charges for falsely claiming U.S. citizenship. The agency said Pérez “chose to leave her two children with an adult at the home.”
Pérez’s attorneys have also filed a request for humanitarian parole and a federal habeas petition calling for her release, she said.

“Why would ICE violate its own rules just to target a nursing mother who has followed all the legal steps of the immigration system?” Nora Ahmed, legal director for the ACLU of Louisiana, said in a statement. “ICE has destroyed a family in the process and is directly responsible for putting children’s lives at risk.”

title: ‘Alien Terrorist Removal Court,’ created in 1996, holds first-ever hearing
summary: The Justice Department is seeking to deport a Texas mom whose kin conspired to launch an ISIS-inspired terrorist attack. She hasn’t been charged with a crime.
story: WASHINGTON — A 47-year-old Texas mom whose son and son-in-law were convicted of conspiring to launch an ISIS-inspired attack made history Thursday by becoming the first person to appear before a court created by Congress in 1996 to speed up the deportation of “alien terrorists.”
Nazira Haji Zada, who has not been charged with a crime, appeared in the Alien Terrorist Removal Court before Chief Judge Joan Ericksen, who normally serves as a federal judge in Minnesota.

Under the framework of the court, the U.S. can attempt to remove noncitizens from the country upon representing them as an alien terrorist under a lower standard than would be required to convict them of a criminal charge. Appeals from that court would be made to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit.
Nazira, who lives in Fort Worth, Texas, had been arrested earlier this week. She was described by the Justice Department as “the matriarch of an alien Afghan family.”
The DOJ filed an application on July 15 to have her removed from the U.S. for her alleged role in a plot to disrupt Election Day in 2024 with a mass shooting.
Nazira was flanked by her lawyers Matthew Farley and Mary Petras of the federal public defender’s office and two translators when she arrived in a federal courtroom in D.C.
“The United States Alien Terrorist Removal Court is now in session,” the clerk announced.

Ericksen, a George W. Bush appointee, quickly noted that Nazira was a lawful permanent resident of the United States and the “first case” to appear before a court that “had laid dormant for three decades.”
“This is not a criminal matter. This is a civil matter,” she said.
Farley immediately attacked the DOJ’s attempt to deport Nazira as unconstitutional. “This entire scheme is in violation of due process and unconstitutional,” he said.
He called the process a violation of Nazira’s rights under the “First, Fourth, Fifth and Sixth” amendments and said the approach was a “runaround of bringing a criminal case.”
Farley also said he’s been reading up on the literature around the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, which lays out some of the reasons why it hasn’t been used in the past.
“I’ve probably read the same law review articles you have,” Ericksen said, joking that there weren’t very many of them.
Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General Hayden O’Byrne laid out the government’s allegations against Nazira and said that her “unsuspecting husband” had no knowledge of the alleged plot.
The government has said in a filing that before emigrating to the U.S., Nazira’s husband “was employed at the Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan from 2009 to 2016.”
Ericksen denied the motion by Nazira’s lawyer for immediate release but said she’d take up the challenges to the proceedings in future hearings.
It remains to be seen whether the Trump administration’s attempt to send Nazira back to Afghanistan by using the ATRC will hold up to constitutional challenges.
Legal scholar John Dorsett Niles wrote in 2008 that in theory it could be considered due process.

“In practice, however, the ATRC has never been used,” Niles wrote. “Perhaps to avoid an adverse constitutional ruling, the attorney general has never brought a deportation proceeding before the court.”
Before the hearing at the federal courthouse in Washington, acting Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the use of the court.

“Congress created the Alien Terrorist Removal Court three decades ago to remove from the United States alien terrorists who never should have been here in the first place,” Blanche said in a statement. “The allegations in this case show the matriarch of an ISIS-sympathizing family aiding in a plot to launch a mass casualty attack on American voters on Election Day.”

When asked if more cases like Nazira’s could wind up being heard in the ATRC, a Justice Department spokesperson said only: “This Department of Justice will use every tool available to bring alien terrorists to justice and remove them from the United States, including this court established by Congress in 1996.”
Nazira landed on the government’s radar after her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, were arrested on Oct. 7, 2024, by authorities in Oklahoma.

Tawhedi had acquired two AK-47-style rifles and 500 rounds of ammunition to target large crowds, the DOJ said. And Tawhedi had conspired with multiple people, including his brother-in-law, Abdullah Haji Zada, for several months to plot out the attack.
Nazira’s son, who was 17 at the time, was charged as an adult and pleaded guilty in April 2024.
Tawhedi, now 28, pleaded guilty to two offenses: conspiring and providing support to the Islamic State group, and attempting to receive firearms to commit a federal crime of terrorism.
But they weren’t the only members of the family who were part of the plot, justice officials argued.

Nazira signed a contract to sell their home and bought “one-way airfare” for her to fly with her remaining children to Kabul, Afghanistan, before the alleged Election Day plot was to be carried out, the government said.
And, according to the DOJ, Nazira had her children pledge their loyalty to the the Islamic State group and “supported” the plot.

title: States push DHS to explain its noncitizen voter claims
summary: Election officials are questioning how the Trump administration arrived at its conclusion that hundreds of thousands of noncitizens appeared on voter rolls across four states.
story: State officials are pushing back on the Department of Homeland Security’s claims that it found tens of thousands of noncitizens on their voter rolls, asking the department to explain how it arrived at its conclusion.

Ahead of President Donald Trump’s primetime speech from the White House earlier this month in which he made sweeping claims of voter fraud, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote to officials in Nevada, Pennsylvania, California and New Jersey, saying he believed the four states had more than 250,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls combined. During a news conference the day after Trump’s speech, Mullin threatened officials with potential prison time if they do not “secure their elections.”

Ahead of Mullin’s requested two-week deadline for response, officials in California, Nevada and Pennsylvania sent back letters questioning where DHS got its data. All three states have declined to share private state voter roll data that includes personal identifying information like Social Security numbers.

“The American public deserves transparency in how their private information is being used at the federal level,” Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat, said in an interview Thursday. “I don’t believe the federal government is being honest with the American people.”

“They’re gathering private information about citizens, but they’re not explaining how they’re doing it, and it may not be accurate. And to classify somebody as not able to exercise their constitutional fundamental rights is a real harm,” Aguilar added.

In separate letters to Mullin dated Wednesday, Aguilar and Pennsylvania Secretary of State Al Schmidt, a Republican, questioned how the federal government arrived at its conclusions without the unredacted voter rolls that the Justice Department has sued each state to obtain.

“How did your department match social security numbers to Nevada registrants and what data sources did you use if not the voter information provided by” the secretary of state, Aguilar wrote in his letter.

“As you know, past analyses of voter lists have relied on faulty methodologies that can lead to inaccurate results and false claims about the citizenship status of eligible voters,” Schmidt wrote. “Please provide a document explaining your methodology, which identifies the data sources you relied on.”
DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the new responses from state officials.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, asked Mullin in a July 23 letter to share the information of anyone who gave the federal government private voter data, as it is a crime under state law.

“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official. Indeed, state law prohibits sharing voters’ sensitive information, including social security numbers, with any person, including the federal government,” Weber wrote.
Weber asked for details on the federal government’s analysis, including data sources and whether artificial intelligence was used.
Noncitizen voting is illegal and rare. Sometimes, noncitizens do end up on states’ voter rolls, but, historically, few have attempted to cast a ballot.

Days after Trump’s speech, Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey, the fourth state singled out by the Trump administration, announced that officials had uncovered a Motor Vehicle Commission error that led to around 6,600 self-identified noncitizens being registered to vote and that roughly 400 cast ballots between 2023 and 2024. The number of noncitizens that New Jersey found on its voter rolls fell short of the 35,000 that DHS claimed.
The Trump administration later asked New Jersey to hand over details on the registrants, but Sherrill said in a letter that the state would not share that information with the federal government.
“DOJ will get this information through all legal means!” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon responded in a post on X on Tuesday.
Sherrill’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Anthony Fauci invokes Fifth Amendment right not to testify at Covid hearing
summary: In his opening statement, the former top health official accused Sen. Rand Paul of having an “unhinged obsession” with him and wanting him put “behind bars.”
story: Dr. Anthony Fauci declined to answer senators’ questions at a contentious hearing Wednesday on the origins of Covid and the government’s handling of the pandemic, saying he would invoke his Fifth Amendment right to avoid the possibility that Republicans would use his testimony to prosecute him for perjury.

The surprise decision set the stage for a hyperpartisan hearing that yielded no new revelations about the origins of the coronavirus or the government response to the pandemic. But the absence of Fauci’s testimony presented plenty of opportunities for Republicans and Democrats to put forth dueling narratives about those issues — and about Fauci himself.

Republicans on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee used their allotted time to criticize Fauci’s recommendations during the Covid pandemic, accusing Fauci, the former head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, of providing harmful advice on issues such as lockdowns and of lacking candor about the origins of the coronavirus.

Democrats came to Fauci’s defense, painting the hearing as a Republican-led effort to entrap him into committing perjury and using their time to focus criticism on the Trump administration’s healthcare policies.

After Fauci had invoked the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times, committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., said as the hearing ended that he would call for a vote to hold him in contempt of Congress. He said after the hearing that the committee would vote on the issue next week.

Paul, a longtime critic of Fauci, has clashed with him numerous times at congressional hearings. Paul has accused him of lying to Congress about the issue of “gain of function” lab research on viruses, which makes them more dangerous to better understand them, and whether funding from the National Institutes of Health ultimately made its way to the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China. Fauci has previously denied the allegations.
On Tuesday, Paul answered a reporter’s question about how he would respond to people who argue that he was trying to put Fauci in a position to perjure himself.

“There’s no risk to perjury if you tell the truth,” Paul said. “In fact, he can even admit to not telling the truth in the past. He can admit destroying records. He can admit to, you know, not adequately presenting both sides of equations, which isn’t really a crime. He can admit to anything. The only thing he can’t do is lie again.”

In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul’s repeated attacks on him formed his rationale for deciding to invoke his Fifth Amendment right. Fauci cited what he characterized as Paul’s “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution, his repeated slanderous comments about me” and his decision to publicly release Fauci’s personal journal.

“The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something — anything — that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words — quote — ‘behind bars,’” Fauci said in his opening remarks.

“Any reasonable person who has followed his unhinged obsession with me would readily come to the same conclusion,” he continued. “Therefore, although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decadeslong record of cooperating with Congress, under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions.”

In the final hours of his administration, former President Joe Biden issued pre-emptive pardons to Fauci and others to shield them from what Biden characterized as potential political prosecutions. This week, Paul did not preclude the possibility that Fauci could face charges over his testimony, saying “we’re going to find out” whether he should be prosecuted.

The pardon was a factor in his legal team’s determination that Fauci should not answer senators’ questions, because Republicans had consistently implied that the pardon would not apply to new statements.

During the hearing, Republican senators repeatedly tried to goad Fauci into responding to their questions — with Josh Hawley, R-Mo., at one point asking him to identify the colors of his tie and the floor’s carpeting.

Fauci answered each question, regardless of the topic, with the same line: “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution.”
At the end of his period of questioning, Paul told Fauci that he would face “repercussions” for not answering.

“The committee will have to consider after this hearing what appropriate action should be taken against you for the failure to testify after being directed to do so,” Paul said. “It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress. There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.”
When Paul concluded, Fauci’s lawyer, David Schertler, tried to say something to the senators but was repeatedly cut off by Paul, who ultimately ordered security to remove him from the committee room.
Shortly after he left the hearing, Schertler told NBC News that Fauci “has a valid Fifth Amendment privilege, and he has the right to assert it.”
“That’s what I was trying to tell the committee, and that’s all I was trying to tell the committee,” he said.
In a separate statement, Schertler called Paul’s actions “outrageous.”
“It proves the baseless and vindictive nature of this proceeding and Rand Paul’s personal vendetta against Dr. Fauci,” he said.
During his time to speak, the top Democrat on the committee, Gary Peters of Michigan, criticized the Republicans’ handling of the hearing, saying he believed the hearing “does real damage.”

“It’s tempting to turn one person into the scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across both the Trump and the Biden administration were responsible for handling,” Peters said, adding that people were facing death threats.
“This is only going to, unfortunately, deter other scientific experts from public service to understand that this is what they would have to go through as they provide their advice to us,” he said.

Separately, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told reporters ahead of his period of questioning that he would not ask Fauci questions, arguing that the “show trial is a perjury craft for criminal prosecution going forward.”
During the hearing, Blumenthal defended Fauci and compared the Republican-led proceedings to Sen. Joseph McCarthy’s anti-communism hearings of the 1950s.

“We should not be part of a rerun of that kind of effort,” Blumenthal said. “This attempt to rebrand one of the most challenging times in our nation’s history is a shortsighted act of desperation that will leave us less prepared for the next pandemic.”

Schertler said in a statement that the circumstances surrounding Fauci’s appearance “regrettably made his continued cooperation impossible,” accusing Paul of taking “an intense and seemingly pathological course of retribution, revenge, and obsession with Dr. Fauci” that has ultimately led to Fauci and his family’s facing threats and harassment.

“Dr. Fauci devoted his lengthy career to saving millions of lives globally through scientific discovery and sound public health policy,” Schertler said in the statement. “The accusations that Chairman Paul continues to propagate are false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable.”

title: This Is What Barack Obama Read and Listened to This Summer — And People Have Thoughts
summary: It’s that time of the year when Barack Obama shares his summer playlist and reading list.
story: It’s that time of the year when Barack Obama shares his summer playlist and reading list.
The former president is known for sharing the books and songs that he has enjoyed over the sunny months, always surprising people with his selections and asking for recommendations.
This year is no different as Obama posted 11 books that captured his attention these past months, as well as a slew of songs that he couldn’t get enough of.

Among the novels that he read include “Kin” by Tayari Jones about two daughters raised without mothers in Honeysuckle, Louisiana. There’s also Ann Patchett’s “Whistler” about a woman who reunites with her stepfather who she hasn’t seen in 40 years. Obama also read Colson Whitehead’s final volume in his “Harlem Trilogy,” “Cool Machine.” The author recently sat down with Craig Melvin for his “Glass Half Full” podcast to discuss the novel.
And when it came to his music selection, Obama treated his social media followers to plenty of hits.

“Here are some of the songs I’ve been listening to this summer,” the former politician captioned his list. “It starts with a song Michelle and I love by Glen Hansard, a great musician who passed tragically this week. Our hearts go out to his family.”

Obama’s taste in music is wide ranging from R&B and rap with “Girl, Get Up” by Doechii and SZA, to rock with “Going Shopping” by The Strokes” to Latin music with Rawayana and Manuel Turizo’s “Inglés en Miami.”
Obama also enjoys classics like Earth, Wind and Fire’s “Can’t Hide Love,” “Modern Love” by David Bowie and “Let’s Get It On” by Marvin Gaye.
Like most years, people paid particular attention to one or two tracks that made it on Obama’s playlist. Many were surprised (and loved) to see “Motion Party” by BossMan Dlow.

“The thought of Obama singing ‘this a motion party you cannot get iiinnnn’ 😭😭😭😭😭,” one person commented, while another added, “Motion Party being on this list is one of the reasons why you’ll always be my President!! 😭😂.”
Even BossMan himself was surprised, commenting, “It’s A Motion Party We Gotta Let Obama Innn.”

Other artists that were included in his playlist also thanked him, including Sheryl Crow who wrote, “Man, I’m super honored that someone I admire so much is listening to a deep deep cut from my second record. Very cool, @barackobama!”
Fred Hammond commented, “Heeeeyyy thank you sir. Truly an honor,” while Anderson .Paak added, “That’s my dog!”
In the comment section of his post, Obama also asked people for suggestions.
“I’m always looking for new songs to listen to, so please share any recommendations in the comments,” he wrote.

title: Karol G Asked a Little Girl What Her Favorite Song Was. The Answer Made the Entire Stadium Laugh
summary: When Karol G asked a young fan at her concert what her favorite song was, she replied that it was “Dai Dai” by Shakira.
story: It was a night to remember for Karol G and one young fan who made the whole stadium smile at the singer’s latest show.

During her July 29 “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour” concert at Rogers Stadium in Toronto, Karol took a moment to say hi to a little girl in the crowd. In video shared by DJ Mechon on Instagram, Karol stopped the music, gave the girl a hug and asked her name.
“Chloe,” she replied, before Karol asked what her favorite song was. “Dai Dai,” the girl replied, referring to Shakira’s song for the World Cup.
“What?” Karol replied, before realizing she was not talking about one of her songs. “’Dai Dai,’ let’s sing it,” she said in Spanish. “She knows it.”
“She just said that her favorite song is ‘Dai Dai’ by Shakira,” Karol continued as the audience laughed. “You want to sing it? You know it?”
The girl then started to sing Shakira’s song, with everyone joining in and Karol cheering her on.

“This was one of the most special moments of the night because it showed both the innocence of children and Karol G’s kindness,” DJ Mechon, who attended the concert and recorded the video, tells TODAY.com. “When she asked the little girl what her favorite song was, she answered ‘Dai Dai,’ which is actually a Shakira song. Rather than making the child feel embarrassed, Karol G embraced the moment, and as the little girl sang, the entire stadium joined in.”

Adding, “It turned into one of the most genuine and heartwarming moments of the concert,” he continued, adding that “being there, for what was probably the biggest Latin concert  Toronto has ever seen, was unforgettable. The energy, emotion, and connection between Karol G and her fans made it a truly special night.”
Julie Haynes, another fan who attended the same concert and shared video of the moment online, also tells TODAY.com that the interaction was among her favorites of the night.

“Out of the whole concert, that was the moment that stuck with me the most. It was so innocent and genuine,” Haynes says. “I love how kids are just unapologetically themselves, and seeing her confidently tell Karol G that her favorite song was ‘Dai Dai’ by Shakira was such a sweet moment I’ll never forget.”
And it was a memorable night for Karol as she became the first female solo artist to headline a show at Rogers Stadium.

The “Latina Foreva” singer kicked off her “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour” on July 27 in Chicago, with fans calling the show a celebration of culture, fawning over her sensational outfits and band on stage.
Just in the past days while on tour, Karol announced her new single, “Matadora,” as well as a new album “No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto.”

During her Toronto concert, she revealed that it will be released on Friday, Aug. 7. The cover art was also unveiled on the screens. She will continue touring across North America, Latin America and Europe, marking her largest live production yet.

title: Are ‘Love Island USA’s’ Aniya And Carl Together? Here’s What They Told Andy Cohen About
summary: Are ‘Love Island USA’s’ Aniya and Carl together after the finale? Are they dating? They just gave a relationship update. Here’s where they stand now.
story: It’s been a few weeks since the “Love Island USA” Season 8 finale aired, and fans are dying to know one question about their faves Aniya Harvey and Carl Schmidt: Are they together or not?
Well, the pair finally has an answer for us.

During a July 29 appearance on Bravo’s late night talk show “Watch What Happens Live,” Aniya and Carl, who were featured alongside the competition winners Trinity Tatum and Bryce Alakai, gave an update on their relationship status.

“We are not officially boyfriend girlfriend yet,” Carl told host Andy Cohen, explaining that he joined the cast during the later half of the season. “I came in late, right? I came in during Casa Amor, so, had a couple weeks to get to know each other.”
Aniya and Carl left the villa at the July 12 finale as the season’s runners-up. Their relationship status had yet to be cemented as their connection was the newest of the final four couples.

Aniya, one of the original cast members, had initially been coupled up with fellow OG cast member KC. However, cracks began to form over time. During the show’s infamously messy Casa Amor episodes at the middle of the season, Aniya, who began to explore a connection with Carl, a bombshell, ultimately chose KC. However, KC explored a connection with bombshell Tierra, with whom he eventually coupled up. Aniya was left single.

In a twist of fate, viewers were invited to vote for two Casa Amor bombshells — one male and one female — who hadn’t been chosen to reenter the villa. Viewers picked Carl, with whom Aniya immediately paired up with once again.

The two spent the last few weeks of the villa sharing some meaningful moments, including meeting one another’s families. During the finale, they were sent on a romantic candlelit and were surprised with a storybook that featured a custom fairytale about their journey together.
“It was always going to be you,” Carl told Aniya during their final moments alone on the show.
During the recent “WWHL” episode, Carl told Cohen that in the two weeks since the islanders have been out of the villa, his connection with Aniya “has just been really strong.”
“We just feel really, really happy,” Carl said. “We just want to kind of keep rolling that as long as we can.”

Season 8 winners Trinity and Bryce — or as the real ones call them, Brinity — are unsurprisingly very much together. The couple, who were the first ones on the show to ever say the three words, “I love you,” confirmed on “WWHL” that they are still inseparable as ever.
The couple joined TODAY on July 15 for their first television appearance after the show wrapped. They told host Craig Melvin that they were dealing with just a touch of “separation anxiety.”

“Something we weren’t anticipating was just like how much our connection has affected us outside of here, too,” Bryce added. “Anytime she’s like, ‘I’m going to go run this errand,’ I’m like, ‘Where’s she going?’ Like, my heart rate starts, I’m like, ‘What’s going on right now?’”

title: Drew Starkey Reacts with Pure Joy at a Surprise Message from DJ Pauly D
summary: Drew Starkey, an unapologetic “Jersey Shore” fan, was surprised with a message from Pauly D during a TODAY appearance on July 30. See the unexpected moment.
story: Drew Starkey, who embraces the “gym, tan and laundry” lifestyle as an unapologetic “Jersey Shore” fan, could not stop smiling when he received a surprise message from his favorite cast member.
The 32-year-old actor stopped by TODAY Thursday, July 30, to chat with Craig Melvin about his new Apple TV series “Lucky” and the upcoming final season of “Outer Banks.”
Toward the end of the interview, Craig playfully mentioned that one of Starkey’s “vices” is his love for reality television.
Starkey confirmed that he is a huge fan of MTV’s “Jersey Shore” and he would love to hang out with star DJ Pauly D one day.
Well, Craig couldn’t make the meet up come true at that moment, but he did have a special gift to reveal: a personal message from the DJ.
“He sent you something,” Craig told Starkey, whose face immediately lit up with pure joy.
“No he did not!” Starkey said in disbelief as the message started to play.

“Yo, what’s up? It’s your boy DJ Pauly D, and this message is for my man, Drew Starkey,” the reality television star said while Starkey clapped his hands and laughed. “What’s up, my dude? Just heard that you are a fan. Well, guess what? I am a fan of you, as well. That’s right.”
Pauly D continued, “I know you live by that ‘gym, tan and laundry’ lifestyle, just like me. I’ve seen you on ‘Outer Banks,’ and I can’t wait to watch the new season.”
The “Jersey Shore” star ended his message by thanking Starkey for his love and support.
When the clip was over, Starkey threw his hands in the air and said, “That’s crazy. GTL, baby. T-shirt time. DJ Pauly D. That’s wild!”
He called the interaction a “full circle” moment.
“You guys make dreams come true,” he added.
Starkey previously revealed he was a member of the “Jersey Shore” fandom in a January 2025 interview with W Magazine where he named the series as his favorite reality show.
“I’m a die-hard ‘Jersey Shore’ girl,” he gushed. “Snooki, DJ Pauly D. It’s my favorite. I’ll go back and watch the OG seasons.”
He shared that the show debuted when he was coming of age.
“‘Jersey Shore’ was such a formative time. I think it came out the summer of my sophomore year of high school. It’s the best,’” he told the magazine.
Starkey recalled his “Jersey Shore” high school days in a behind-the-scenes interview with TODAY after his talk with Craig.
“T-shirt tiiimmmeee,” he said in a clip, referencing a line from Season One of the show.
“My friends and I were screaming ‘T-shirt time’ all summer when that came out,” the actor said.
Another favorite phrase? GTL, of course.

title: Sandra Oh Says Her ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ Role Inspired Fan to Dump Her Partner, Go Into Law
summary: Sandra Oh is revealing how her “Grey’s Anatomy” character Dr. Cristina Yang still influences devoted fans today.
story: Although Sandra Oh’s Dr. Cristina Yang hasn’t stepped foot in a Seattle hospital for over a decade, the beloved character still has a huge impact on longtime “Grey’s Anatomy” fans.

Though the 55-year-old actor, who has repeatedly confirmed throughout the years that she will never return to the show, still has a soft spot for her character. During her latest podcast appearance on the July 28 episode of “Dinner’s On Me with Jesse Tyler Ferguson”, Oh discussed her character’s connection to fans, sharing one particularly memorable interaction.

She told host and actor Jesse Tyler Ferguson that “young people” approach her “all the time” to praise her “Grey’s Anatomy” character. For example, last year, when Oh was performing in the opera “La Fille du Régiment” at the Metropolitan Opera House, she chatted with a fan who had a meaningful story to share.

“She came up to me and she goes, ‘I have to tell you something,’” Oh recalled. “She was saying, ‘10 years ago I was watching your show and I was going to get married to this guy and he didn’t want me to work. He was like, I’ll take care of you, blah blah blah.’ And she was quoting this scene.”
Oh told Ferguson that the fan went on to describe how much one particular episode, along with the character of Cristina Yang, impacted the fan to make a drastic life change.
“And she goes, ‘I left him. I became a lawyer.’”

Oh said that just a few moments into the interaction, she knew the exact scene the fan was describing. She remembered a Season 10 episode in which Cristina’s ex-fiancé Preston Burke, portrayed by Isaiah Washington, returned with a job opportunity for her all the way in Switzerland. Cristina had assumed that her ex-beau was offering her a position to work with him at the Klausman Institute for Medical Research in Zurich. Instead, Preston offered her the chance to helm the institute.
In the season, which ended up May 2014, Cristina made a major move, eventually deciding to pack her bags and leave Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital for the new opportunity.
Oh said she approved of the fan’s decision and also gave her some sage advice.

“I was just like, ‘Good for you. Whatever was going on in your life, it was not enough. And that guy who was saying that you are not going to be who you’re going to be and fulfill your destiny and go become a lawyer. Leave that,’” she recalled telling the fan.
Oh said the conversation emphasized her role as an actor and the power of good storytelling.

“What we need to do is just plant seeds for things to grow, that hopefully some young woman when she’s, like, 25 decides, ‘F— that s— man. I’m going to leave you and I’m going to become my own woman and be in charge of my life and not depend on you.’”
Oh portrayed the fan-favorite surgeon for 10 seasons before departing the medical drama. During Oh’s time on the show, she earned one Golden Globe and two Screen Actors Guild awards.
“Grey’s Anatomy” continues to run and will return for its 23rd season in the fall.
The actor has previously mentioned how much she values Cristina Yang and the character’s lasting impact.
In May 2021, Oh said on the Los Angeles Times’ “Asian Enough” podcast that it was “rare” to see Cristina Yang remain relevant in pop culture years later.
She also explained why she does not want to reprise the role.

“I left that show, my God, seven years ago almost,” she said at the time. “So in my mind, it’s gone. But for a lot of people it’s still very much alive. And while I understand and I love it, I have moved on.”

During her talk with Ferguson, Oh also revealed the decision to move on came after Season 9 when creator Shonda Rhimes pulled her aside and asked if she wanted to stay on the show. Oh took some time to contemplate her decision and followed her “creative being.”

“I felt very much like I did my job. I really did my job. I feel like I created a full character. I feel I grew the character 10 years time where it’s a believable growth,” Oh explained. “And the privilege was to actually plan an exit.”
She called it a “gift” from the show’s writers to give her character a thoughtful sendoff.

title: ‘Idaho Murders’ Doc Shows ‘Something That Nobody’s Really Seen Before,’ Director Says
summary: Skye Borgman, the documentarian behind Netflix’s Idaho Murders documentary, looks at the true story that inspired it and what makes it so moving.
story: A fun college night out. A horrific discovery by police. A heartbreaking sequence of phone calls to family members.

The vibrant lives and tragic deaths of four Idaho college students are put in context in the new three-episode Netflix docuseries, “The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare,” which was released on July 29.

The docuseries aims to show viewers more about the lives of University of Idaho students Madison Mogen, 21; Kaylee Goncalves, 21; Xana Kernodle, 20; and Ethan Chapin, 20, whom authorities say were stabbed to death at an off-campus house on Nov. 13, 2022. In the series, police bodycam footage from the aftermath of the 911 call is woven with interviews with family, friends and law enforcement to paint a full picture of the case.

It also hits Netflix just two days after Bryan Kohberger, the former doctoral student who pleaded guilty in July 2025 to killing the four students, filed a petition in an Idaho court. He has requested to rescind his guilty plea because he said he is innocent and wants a trial.

TODAY.com spoke with “The Idaho Murders” director Skye Borgman about the latest documentary involving the case. The murders were also the subject of 2025 documentaries released on Peacock and Prime Video as well as a 2025 episode of NBC’s “Dateline.”
“I think it adds a fair amount of extra that we don’t know about,” Borgman said about the Netflix series she directed.
A trove of police bodycam footage and documents about the investigation were publicly released after Kohberger pled guilty in July 2025.

“It’s out there, you can find it, but not in a way where it’s been put together that shows what was happening the night before, what was happening the next day, how these families were informed,” Borgman said. “All of that, put together, is something that nobody’s really seen before.”
‘There to Change the World’: Shining a Light on the 4 Students Who Were Killed
The film also uses video shot by the students and their friends to show candid moments as they enjoy college life, bond with one another and talk about the future.
The sweet relationship between Chapin and Kernodle, who were a couple, is shown alongside the close friendship between Goncalves and Mogen.

“Talking to Tami (Buttz), Kaylee’s aunt, she said, ‘I want these kids to be remembered for who they were, not just victims,’” Bergman said. “And I said, ‘Well, let’s do that. Let’s see them having the time of their life in college, let’s be with them in the bar, let’s be drunk with them, let’s be happy with them, let’s be in love with them, let’s know who they were.

“And I think it magnifies the loss in such an insane and intense way, but it also really shows us that these people were there to change the world, and they were really amazing, incredible, intelligent people.”
A Chilling Look at the Aftermath
The docuseries begins with bodycam footage of police coming into the house after a 911 call and discovering the bodies of the four slain students.

“This moment in time is what changed everything,” Borgman said. “This 911 call that came through, it was devastating for the people who made the call, it was devastating for the community, and it was devastating for the families. And it really is that day that just changed the course of so many people’s lives. Using that footage in the beginning, I wanted to really put us into that space to know how devastating it was for everybody involved.”

Ed Jacobson, a former FBI special agent involved in the investigation, says in the documentary that Goncalves and Mogen were sleeping on the third floor of the off-campus house in Moscow when they were stabbed to death. Chapin and his girlfriend, Kernodle, were then fatally stabbed while in a bedroom on the second floor.
Jacobson reveals that Kernodle fought back against the killer after being stabbed.
“She had over 50 stab wounds on her,” Jacobson says in the docuseries. “She put up a fight.”

There were also two more roommates in the house, Bethany Funke and Dylan Mortensen, who were not harmed. They called police after hearing sounds upstairs during the night and then called police. They were not interviewed for the documentary, but video of their interviews with police are included.
In one heartbreaking sequence, friends, neighbors and family across the country are shown trying to comprehend the incomprehensible as they each separately learn about what happened.
Portraying a Killer and the 1 Question the Docuseries Can’t Answer
Bryan Kohberger’s name is not mentioned until well into the docuseries when police announce they have a suspect in custody.

“From the beginning I wanted it to be victim-forward,” Borgman said about the series. “And what that meant was holding off as long as possible until we showed images of the perpetrator, before we spoke his name. We tried to show the fewest amount of images as possible, we tried to speak his name the fewest amount possible. The families do not speak his name — they will never speak his name — so I wanted to honor that as much as we could.”

His scant online presence is examined by law enforcement and forensic experts, who say in the docuseries that it appeared to be intentional. Evidence used by investigators to track down Kohberger, including surveillance video footage of a vehicle near the scene and a knife sheath Kohberger purchased on Amazon, is also detailed.

The one question no one has been able to answer in any of the documentaries and specials is why the killer committed the murders. Kohberger did not have to reveal any motive or address the court when he pleaded guilty to the killings in 2025.

“I think I was hoping to, through the course of making this series and spending close to three years on it, have some sort of answers as to why,” Borgman said. “Why would he do this? Sitting and talking to the FBI agent, he was like, ‘You’re never going to have those answers.’”

“Everybody wants to know why,” she continued. “Why these four? Why this house? There was zero personal connection, and we have to kind of be OK with never having those answers. And I think the same is true for why he made some of the mistakes or some of the things that led law enforcement to finally find him. I think maybe there is a little bit of hubris involved. Maybe he thought he could get away with the perfect crime. Maybe he thought he was untouchable. Maybe he just in the moment kind of forgot certain things. I don’t know the answer to it, and I don’t think we ever will.”
Kohberger said in a statement to The New York Times on July 27 that the account state investigators laid out in court documents was a “myopic narrative” and a “work of fiction.”
Several families share their frustration in the docuseries that the state accepted a guilty plea instead of forcing him to go to trial, while others say they felt relief there was some closure.

One of the most emotional parts of the series comes when family members give victim impact statements in court with Kohberger sitting there after he pled guilty. Goncalves’ older sister, Alivea Goncalves, is shown delivering a fiery speech.
“You are not profound, you are pathetic,” she says. “You aren’t special or deep, not mysterious or exceptional. Don’t ever get it twisted again.”
Borgman is hoping that by presenting the full picture of the students who were killed she can join their families in preserving their memories.

“I’m impressed as hell at the families and their resilience and determination and stamina and belief that they can make a difference,” Borgman said. “They’re taking this terrible tragedy and turning it into something positive for other families, and they have this purpose now. I’m honored to be able to tell this story.”

title: Jenny Jackson Knew ‘Yesteryear’ Would Be a Hit. How She Won the Author Over
summary: Jenny Jackson spoke to Jenna on an episode of Open Book with Jenna about her new book The Shampoo Effect and working with Caro Claire Burke for Yesteryear.
story: Jenny Jackson has a double life in the literary world.
A bestselling author, her debut “Pineapple Street” was a breakout hit in 2023. Her second, “The Shampoo Effect,” was chosen as a Read With Jenna book this month.

She’s also an accomplished editor. Jackson is the editorial director of fiction at Knopf, where she’s worked with the likes of Gabrielle Zevin (“Tomorrow and Tomorrow and Tomorrow”), Kevin Kwan (“Crazy Rich Asians”) and Emily St. John Mandel (“Station Eleven”).

Jackson sat down with Jenna for the July 30 episode of her “Open Book with Jenna” podcast to talk through the balancing act and what goes into the making of a hit, like this year’s “Yesteryear” by Caro Claire Burke.
“If Jenny Jackson gets a book, you know it’s going to be good,” Jenna said.
Jackson said she went to great lengths to nab “Yesteryear,” which follows a trad wife who seemingly lands back in the 1800s to have to live out the lifestyle she’s trying to emulate.

“We knew we had something special on our hands,” Jackson said of the book. “I love-bombed the author. I mailed her flowers, we went to auction and I bid the absolute most and ended up with it. I felt this level of passion because it was doing something so intense and so different.”

“Yesteryear” spent multiple weeks at No. 1 on the New York Times hardcover fiction bestseller list. It’s also headed to the screen. Over a year before it came out, Amazon MGM Studios picked up the novel for a screen adaptation, with Anne Hathaway set to lead.
Jenna inquired about the “secret sauce” that Jackson is looking for when she’s acquiring titles for Knopf.

“I’m always looking for a book that is doing something I haven’t read lately, or I haven’t ever read before,” Jackson explained. “A lot of our industry thrives on recommendations that are very similar to other books that are hot in the market. Unfortunately, if you try and publish that way, you’re always going to be two years behind the trends.”
Or, to sum it up: “I would rather publish a book that half the people love and half the people hate, than a book that 90% of people like a lot,” she said.
She said “Yesteryear” is a great example of a divisive novel that gets people talking, precisely because not everyone loves it.

“I’ve seen a lot of people talking about ‘Yesteryear,’ specifically saying, ‘I don’t like it.’ And I’ve realized what often that means is it made me uncomfortable. I think that people are not always willing to feel uncomfortable, but I think it’s really good for us to feel uncomfortable, because that means we’re exposing ourselves to different worldviews, which is going to hopefully, in time, build empathy and build connection,” she said.
Jackson told Jenna she plans to keep working as an editor and writer for the foreseeable future.

“I am unwilling to give either up. And I’ve had a few people say, like, ‘OK, when is the moment? You have two bestsellers. When is the moment where you feel like you can quit being an editor?’ And I laugh, I’m like, ‘Why would I want to do that?’ I love my work. I have the best job in the world. I’m never going to quit.”

title: BTS Chooses Not to Submit to the Grammys After New Asian Pop Category Announced
summary: Why K-pop group BTS will not be submitting their music to next year’s Grammy Awards, the members announced July 28.
story: K-pop group BTS will not be submitting their music to next year’s Grammy Awards, the members announced July 28.
The group — made up of members RM, Jimin, V, Suga, Jungkook, Jin and J-Hope — shared the same statement on their individual Instagram stories.

The announcement comes just over a month after the Recording Academy — the body of musicians, producers, engineers and more that vote on the awards, announced five new categories — including a “Best Asian Pop Music Performance,” which would include K-pop among other genres.

“We have decided not to enter the Grammys this year,” reads a translation of the message, which was written in Korean. “I hope that music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.”

In a statement shared with TODAY.com, Grammys CEO Harvey Mason Jr. said that he was “saddened” to hear BTS’ decision, but understood and respected the choice. Mason also said that artists who submit to a genre category — such as Asian pop, jazz or country — are not excluded from also submitting to, and being considered in, the general field categories. These categories include record of the year, album of the year and song of the year.

“Those categories remain open to any eligible recording, regardless of genre,” Mason said in the statement. “Recognition in a genre category and recognition in the General Field are not mutually exclusive. An artist can absolutely pursue both.”
Mason also said that the Asian pop category was “created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth” of pop music out of Asia.
“More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized,” Mason said in the statement.

According to the Academy’s description of the new categories, which was announced on June 16, the best Asian pop music performance would recognize performances “originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets.” This would include K-pop, J-pop, C-pop and more, and involve the “meaningful use of one or more Asian languages.”

BTS, which stands for Bangtan Sonyeondan, or Bulletproof Boy Scouts, would have been able to submit work off of their newest album “Arirang,” which came out in March. The album marks the group’s first album together after each of the members completed their mandatory military service in Korea.

The group has a special spot in Grammys history. In 2019, they became the first K-pop act to present at the prestigious awards show. The group, which presented the best R&B album, had the honor of handing the award to winner H.E.R. for her self-titled album.
“Growing up in South Korea, we always dreamed of being on the Grammys stage,” said bandmember RM, according to Variety. “Thank you to all our fans for making this dream come true and we’ll be back.”

A year later, they became the first K-pop act to perform at the awards show, putting on a stunning performance alongside rapper Lil Nas X for the hit “Old Town Road.” And in 2022, they performed the hit single “Butter,” which has racked up more than 115 million views on YouTube alone.

They’ve also earned five Grammy award nominations, including three for best pop duo/group performance and one best music video nod for 2013’s “Yet to Come (The Most Beautiful Moment).” While they were the first K-pop group to receive any Grammy nods, they have yet to win an award.

Most recently, the group made headlines for their performance at the World Cup Finals halftime show on July 19. Dressed in black, white and red coordinating ensembles, BTS took over the pitch with an electrifying performance of their song “Dynamite.”

title: ‘Tony’ Reviews: Here’s What Critics Are Saying About the Anthony Bourdain Biopic
summary: Here’s what critics are saying about the Anthony Bourdain biopic, “Tony.”
story: Anthony Bourdain takes center stage in “Tony,” a biopic of the late chef and author.

In the film, Dominic Sessa, known for his work in the Academy Award-winning 2023 comedy-drama “The Holdovers,” as well as 2025’s “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t,” fills the role of a young, blunt Bourdain. The film, directed by Matt Johnson, also stars Antonio Banderas, Emilia Jones and Leo Woodall.
Bourdain died by suicide in 2018, yet the author — who wrote bestselling 2000 book “Kitchen Confidential,” which rocketed him to stardom — continues to inspire fans to this day.
“Tony” takes moviegoers back to a 19-year-old Bourdain in the summer of 1975, when he worked at a seafood restaurant in Cape Cod, Massachusetts.
The film, which has a 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes as of July 29, opens Aug. 7 and is poised to take a bite out of the box office.
Thinking of checking it out? Here’s what the critics are saying.
The Hollywood Reporter
“A slender slice of a famous life, the movie feels a little wispy in its mix of scrappy and sweet, rough-edged and yet bathed in the balming glow of nostalgia,” David Rooney writes.
“But it has an idiosyncratic charm that fits the title character, without ever sanding down the abrasive side of a chronic liar or masking his insecurities.”
Rooney also praised Sessa’s performance.

“Making good on his promise in ‘The Holdovers,’ Dominic Sessa is excellent in the role, nailing the contradictory aspects of a slippery character while mapping his coming-of-age arc with empathy and honesty,” he writes.
“There’s no dark foreshadowing of the tragedy we know will come 43 years later — only chutzpah, raw potential and intermittent flickers of vulnerability.”
The Daily Beast

Nick Schager’s review echoed the sentiment that Sessa holds his own in the film, noting it “becomes more convincing and authentic with each passing scene, it has a rough-around-the-edges charm that’s in keeping with its go-for-broke protagonist.”
Schager also cites the film’s “spontaneity and genuineness” and lauds Banderas’ work.

“‘Tony’ swings and sways like a lobster boat in choppy waters off the New England coast, and though that setting would seem to be an unlikely place to find Antonio Banderas, the star makes for a delightful boss and, eventually, mentor,” he writes.

Schager says “Tony” serves as a “prologue” for the success Bourdain would later find, calling it a “tad slight” when considering the rich life Bourdain eventually led. However, the film is successful when assessed in its own “limited terms.”
“It may be little more than a tease that leads viewers to Bourdain’s copious written and screen works, but as far as amuse-bouches go, ‘Tony’ is a memorably tasty one,” he writes.
Variety
Owen Gleiberman opens his review, pondering “what Bourdain himself would have made of the movie.”
“To me, if an Anthony Bourdain biopic can’t clear the bar called ‘Bourdain would have liked it,’ it’s probably not a good movie,” he continues. “‘Tony’ clears that bar.”
He also applauds Johnson’s directorial effort.

“‘Tony’ has been framed as the origin story of how Anthony Bourdain became Anthony Bourdain,” he writes. “But one of the many things that Matt Johnson ... understands is that Anthony — or, as he called himself then, Tony — already was Anthony Bourdain.”
Gleiberman said the film marks a watershed moment for Sessa.

“To me, one of the most pleasurable things in movies is that moment when you see an actor become a movie star,” he writes “That’s what happens to Dominic Sessa in ‘Tony.’ I don’t care if the film is a summer indie smash or not (though it deserves to be) — it shows you that Sessa has the goods.”
The Wrap
William Bibbiani’s review begins by comparing “Tony” to “The Social Network,” explaining how the biopic understands “how to really make us care about” a person who is not necessarily appealing.
“‘Tony’ never makes young Bourdain entirely likable,” he writes later.

“This isn’t a superhero origin story where he changes and becomes a do-gooder at the end,” he continues. “This is an origin story about Bourdain’s inciting incident, the exact moment in his life where he realized he needed to change. In Matt Johnson’s hands, that’s epic enough for a whole film.”
Still, the movie left him feeling somewhat hollow.

“By the time the credits roll, ‘Tony’ has long since receded in a formula,” he writes. “The big finale feels contrived and a little unconvincing. I guess the filmmakers thought subverting the tone of a biopic was enough, so Johnson throws Bourdain’s fan base a bone. It just doesn’t have any meat on it.”
The film, Bibbiani goes on to write, does however earn the viewer’s affection — “mostly because it never pretends Bourdain has.”

“We are invited to view the genius as a work in progress. Bourdain’s rough draft stinks; the film about this rough draft is polished and interesting, but another round of notes wouldn’t have killed it,” he writes. “We’re watching a guy who will one day reach his full potential, in a movie that doesn’t entirely reach its own.”
Associated Press
Mark Kennedy’s opening paragraph takes a big swing at a missed opportunity.
“Like all first courses, it leaves you with a nice first taste — but still hungry,” he writes.
Kennedy writes that the film’s director and co-writer Matt Johnson took “liberties with a formative period in Bourdain’s life.”
However, he “still only manages to tell the story of how a callow lad became somewhat of a less callow lad after toiling in a restaurant kitchen on Cape Cod in 1975,” Kennedy writes.
Kennedy laments how this picture could’ve been even better.
“In ‘Tony,’ the world-weary, forever romantic, noodle-slurping Bourdain that we would fall in love with decades later via travel shows like “Parts Unknown” stays firmly out of grasp,” he writes.
Kennedy also asks whether it was necessary to place Bourdain at the center of this film.
“Who doesn’t like a good coming of age?” Kennedy writes. “Why did it have to be Bourdain if Bourdain never gets to be Bourdain?”
ScreenRant
Matt Harrison credits the film, which he calls “laugh-out-loud funny” for making an entertaining flick with Bourdain as the central character.
“It works on its own terms, with or without the halo of its subject’s career. It’s actually about something. And it’s a delight to watch,” he writes.
“It’s sincerely interested in who this lost 19-year-old thinks he is, who he actually is, and who he’s going to choose to become,” he adds.

Harrison, who calls the film “thoroughly enjoyable,” also singled out how the scenes in the kitchen feel “truly alive.” And Sessa “can embody all the epigraph’s unlikable traits and remain remarkably easy to root for.”
IndieWire
“‘Tony’ retains the sincere flavor of street meat despite being factory-processed within an inch of its life,” David Ehrlich writes.
He also salutes Sessa’s “wholly self-possessed lead performance” and how Johnson framed one of the early and key parts of Bourdain’s journey.

“Johnson recognizes how this, at heart, is a coming-of-age story about a rising star who’s learning to be unburdened by a future that’s better than he could ever imagine — a kid who’s learning that no one can become the person they pretend to be without being the person they actually are along the way,” he writes.
“‘Tony’ struggles for an ending, but it doesn’t really need one; the real fun here lies in paving the way to parts unknown.”

title: The Nickname Robert Pattinson’s Daughter Has For ‘The Batman’ Star Is Too Cute
summary: Musician Suki Waterhouse said that her 2-year-old daughter, whom she shares with fiancé Robert Pattinson, isn’t really bothered by Pattinson’s slightly scary costume and makeup that he wears while playing Batman.
story: Musician Suki Waterhouse said that her 2-year-old daughter, whom she shares with fiancé Robert Pattinson, isn’t really bothered by Pattinson’s slightly scary costume and makeup that he wears while playing Batman.
In fact, it seems the toddler is embracing her dad’s alter-ego.
During an appearance on a recent episode of the “And The Writer Is” podcast, Waterhouse, 34, revealed the sweet nickname the toddler uses when she sees Pattinson, 40, as the vigilante.
“She calls him, like, ‘Daddy Batman’ now because he’s always dressed up like that for the next seven months whenever he’s on FaceTime,” said the singer, who gave birth to the baby girl in 2024.
During the podcast episode, Waterhouse opened up about being a mom, revealing how her daughter processes her parents’ unique jobs.
The couple have not publicly revealed their daughter’s name.

The songwriter told host fellow musician Ross Golan that her daughter understands that Waterhouse is a musician and that her dad dons a cape and mask to portray Batman. She shared the funny moment that she and her daughter had on FaceTime with Pattinson, who called them from the set of the long-anticipated “The Batman” sequel, “The Batman Part II,” which is currently in production.
“She’s on FaceTime to her dad who today is covered in blood with huge black circles around his eyes and I’m like, ‘Hi, is it fine?’ And we’re just like, ‘It’s fine,’” she told Golan.

While Pattinson is away filming, Waterhouse has been enjoying some mother-daughter bonding time. She shared on the podcast that she and her daughter were flipping through a book the other day, when the toddler spotted a girl holding a guitar.
“She was like, ‘That’s your job,’” she recalled to Golan.
Waterhouse said her daughter had been watching her play guitar and practice her set as she prepared for her “Loveland Tour,” which kicked off on July 22 in Phoenix, Arizona.
“She’ll say, like, ‘mommy songs’ (and) I’ll show her my music videos and stuff and so it’s cool,” she continued.
Waterhouse added that her daughter enjoys sitting in on glam sessions with her hair and makeup team and looking at the different nail polish options.
Waterhouse and Pattinson, who were first spotted together in 2018, have both opened up about their family and the experience of raising a daughter.
When Waterhouse stopped by TODAY in December 2024, she gushed that she was “completely and utterly besotted” with her baby girl.
“I didn’t know that it would be this good,” she said.
After her appearance, she spoke with TODAY.com and talked about how excited she was to be taking her daughter on tour for the first time.
She explained, “There’s so many hours before you get on stage of walking around, being in a different city — doing that with her will be amazing.”
Waterhouse also shared that her favorite moment of the day was playing in the pool with her daughter and fiancé.

“We have, like, a routine of putting her in the swimming pool and jumping in and out of the pool,” she said. “That’s just always the most fun, like, end of the day, 5 p.m., we all get in the pool and be silly. It’s amazing.”
Pattinson has also talked about parenthood, discussing how he has grown since becoming a father in an interview with Icon Magazine published in October 2025.
The proud dad said, “I have so much more patience. It’s funny, it’s not even patience; I genuinely enjoy hanging out with babies. That surprised me.”

He playfully added, “It’s also funny how you start having real, normie conversations — about things like schools or daycares… it’s so strange. It’s like, there’s this gravitational pull…Like, I have to wear Patagonia puffer jackets and cargo shorts now. I just have to.”

title: What Happens to Drew Starkey’s Character Cary in ‘Lucky’?
summary: Does Cary die in Lucky? What happens to Cary in Lucky? Here’s a recap of Episode 4 of the Apple TV series “Lucky”.
story: Warning: Spoilers ahead for “Lucky.”

“You’re alive. Good for you,” are the first words Lucky utters to her husband Cary after finding him hiding out in a luxurious beachside home while she has been fighting to survive ever since he left.

“Lucky,” the Apple TV miniseries based on Marissa Stapley’s novel of the same name starring Anya Taylor-Joy as the titular character, opened with the protagonist being abandoned by her husband, played by Drew Starkey, after the two stole $10 million and planned to run off together.

In the first three episodes of the crime thriller, Lucky is on the run, dodging the FBI and her mother-in-law Priscilla, (Annette Bening) who happens to be a crime boss. The con artist is looking for answers, too, as she tries to track down her deceitful spouse and figure out why he betrayed her.

Her answers arrive in Episode 4, out July 29, when Lucky and Cary come face-to-face for the first time. During an intense and bloody confrontation, Cary reveals why he left his wife confused and alone, and what happened to the money. His revelation leads to a heartbreaking scene at the end of the episode that sets up Lucky’s journey for the rest of the season.
Read on to find out where Cary has been and what happens to his character below.
Why Did Cary Leave Lucky?

When Cary walks into his hideout and finds his scorned wife waiting for him, he admits he knew she would track him down. He attempts to explain his actions and make amends. But she isn’t interested at first, instead punching him in the face after he approaches her.

Lucky berates him for leaving her scared and vulnerable and accuses him of never loving her. He apologizes and assures her their relationship is real. He reveals that he left because his mom planned to kill Lucky.

We learn in a flashback scene that Cary previously visited his mom and she shared that she knew Lucky had stolen millions from her. Priscilla also learned that Lucky had turned her in to the FBI, sending her to prison for years. Cary calls Lucky out for keeping that secret from him throughout their marriage.

Despite feeling hurt, Cary still wanted to protect his wife. So, he drugged her after their night out in Las Vegas, took the money and left their hotel room in the wee hours of the morning. When he reached his mom, he changed his mind and decided to return to Lucky. But when he arrived at the hotel, he saw the building was surrounded by police and drove away.
Cary took the money and deposited most of it into a Bitcoin account, protected by a seed phrase. He used the rest of the money to purchase his secret spot in La Jolla, California.

When Lucky asks for the phrase and he refuses, she threatens to shoot him. Before she can pull the trigger, the FBI, led by Agent Billie Rand (Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor), bang on the door and demand Cary come outside.
Does Lucky Forgive Cary?
As the FBI enter, Lucky and Cary flee in their getaway car.

A high-speed hunt ensues through the streets of San Diego. Just when Cary and Lucky think they have evaded the authorities, they run into Priscilla, who also starts chasing them. Then, the police are on their trail again.
Possibly facing death, Lucky confesses to her husband that she still loves him. “I don’t regret us,” she tells him.
“Neither do I,” he replies.
Does Cary Die?
Unfortunately, yes.

Cary decides to slow down the police by leaning out the window and attempting to shoot the tires of the cop cars. He and the police exchange fire. When one of the tires on Cary and Lucky’s car is shot, the vehicle flips over multiple times.
Lucky awakes and sees that while Cary survived the crash, he was shot by one of the officers. She tries to stop the bleeding and keep him alive, but it doesn’t work.
“You were happy…” he tells her before his eyes close and he dies.
What Will Happen in Episode 5?
With no time to mourn the death of her husband, Lucky sneaks out of the vehicle and goes on the run once more.

With only three episodes remaining, including the finale out on Aug. 19, viewers will see if Lucky will manage to stay alive and how she will retrieve the money now that Cary died without sharing the seed phrase.
Plus, viewers will likely watch Lucky and Priscilla face off and see how she’ll get help from her dad John (Timothy Olyphant) despite him being in prison.
Episode 5, titled “Are We Bad People?” will be released on Aug. 5.

title: Fabien Frankel Talks Shocking ‘House of the Dragon’ Twist: ‘I Knew I Had it Coming’
